signals.title: [Bug]: GLM-5.2 MTP accepts 0% of drafts on MI355X (gfx950); disabling expert parallelism hits hipErrorIllegalAddress
signals.text: ### Your current environment `collect_env.py` output isn't available (the nodes were tied up); details taken from the container image and run logs: ``` vLLM : 0.27.1+rocm723 PyTorch : 2.11.0+gitd0c8b1f ROCm : 7.2.3 Container : vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.27.1 GPU : 8x AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950) amdgpu : 6.16.13, kernel 6.8.0-137-generic Model : amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 (quark MXFP4) MoE backend: aiter ``` ### 🐛 Describe the bug GLM-5.2 MTP starts fine on MI355X and then accepts **zero** draft tokens. Speculative decoding is pure overhead — it drafts at ~40-230 tok/s and accepts none of it. ```bash export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=1 vllm serve /models/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \ --served-model-name amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \ --trust-remote-code \ --async-scheduling \ --distributed-executor-backend mp \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.80 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --max-num-seqs 2 \ --moe-backend aiter \ --compilation-config '{"mode":3,"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE"}' \ --tool-call-parser glm47 --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --no-disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' ``` Startup resolves as expected — target `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`, draft `DeepSeekMTPModel` — then: ``` SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted throughput: 0.00 tokens/s, Drafted throughput: 37.80 tokens/s, Accepted: 0 tokens, Drafted: 378 tokens, Per-position acceptance rate: 0.000, 0.000, 0.000, Avg Draft acceptance rate: 0.0% ``` What I tried: | # | change | result | |---|---|---| | A | as above | `acceptance length 1.00`, per-position `0.000, 0.000, 0.000` | | B | `num_speculative_tokens: 1` | `acceptance length 1.00`, per-position `0.000` | | C | `--kv-cache-dtype auto` | `acceptance length 1.05`, per-position `0.046, 0.000, 0.000` | | D | drop `--enable-expert-parallel` | crashes, see below | B rules out the startup warning's explanation: ``` WARNING [speculative.py:912] Enabling num_speculative_tokens > 1 will run multiple times on same MTP layer, which may result in lower acceptance rate ``` Position 0 is 0.000 at `num_speculative_tokens=1` too, so re-running GLM-5.2's single nextn layer isn't what's breaking this — the very first draft token is never accepted. C says fp8 KV contributes but isn't the cause: bf16 KV lifts position 0 from 0.000 to ~0.05, still far from usable. D, without expert parallelism, dies during memory profiling instead: ``` terminate called after throwing an instance of 'c10::AcceleratorError' Search for `hipErrorIllegalAddress' in https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/HIP/en/latest/index.html Exception raised from ~CUDAGraph at /app/pytorch/aten/src/ATen/hip/HIPGraph.cpp:302 ``` I also checked whether the unquantized nextn layer is being mis-handled by the quark loader — it isn't, as far as I can tell. Layer 78 is genuinely unquantized in this checkpoint (789 `.weight`, 0 `.weight_scale`, 781 entries in `quantization_config.exclude`), but `DeepSeekMTPModel` sets `mtp_start_layer_idx = num_hidden_layers` and names it `model.layers.78`, which is what the exclude patterns match on. So the exclusions should apply. For reference, SGLang on the same node with the same checkpoint gets a working draft: ``` Decode batch, #running-req: 1, ..., accept len: 3.00, accept rate: 0.67, cuda graph: True ``` This may be the same root cause as #48568 (MI300X / gfx942), which points at MTP's `mtp_block` reduce-scattering under `--enable-expert-parallel` with TP>1 while the predictor layer doesn't restore full tokens. Filing separately because the symptom here is different in a way that matters: on gfx950 there's no hang and no error — it silently produces a 0% acceptance rate, so a benchmark run looks healthy and just reports worse numbers. Disabling EP also fails differently (illegal address rather than working around it). Happy to run further diagnostics on gfx950 if that helps. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] I have searched for similar issues and read the [documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/).

signals.title: [Bug]: Prefill misdispatched into spec-decode FULL cudagraph when prompt length == 1 + num_speculative_tokens → silent GDN state loss, garbage output (hybrid/Qwen3-Next models)
signals.text: ## Summary When speculative decoding is enabled, a **prefill** whose scheduled token count happens to equal `uniform_decode_query_len * num_reqs` is misclassified as a uniform-decode batch and dispatched into the **FULL cudagraph captured for spec-decode**. For hybrid models with GDN/linear-attention layers (e.g. Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5-MoE), this silently skips **all recurrent-state writes** for that request: every subsequent decode step then computes from a zero initial state, producing deterministic garbage output and a collapsed draft acceptance rate. The trigger is absurdly easy to hit: with `num_speculative_tokens=2`, **any 3-token prompt** (e.g. the Chinese prompt `中国的首都是` under the Qwen tokenizer) poisons the request from its very first step. I have root-caused this with per-block checksums of the GDN state pools and verified a one-line-of-logic fix. Code on current `main` is identical to what I debugged on 0.27.1. ## Root cause `GPUModelRunner._is_uniform_decode` (vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py) is a **pure shape check**: ```python return ( ((max_num_scheduled_tokens == uniform_decode_query_len) and (num_tokens == max_num_scheduled_tokens * num_reqs)) if force_uniform_decode is None else force_uniform_decode ) ``` With MTP `k=2`, `uniform_decode_query_len = 1 + 2 = 3`. A virgin single request whose prompt is exactly 3 tokens gives `max_num_scheduled_tokens == 3` and `num_tokens == 3 * 1`, so the **prefill** is classified as uniform decode and `cudagraph_dispatcher.dispatch(..., uniform_decode=True)` routes it into the FULL graph captured for spec-decode. The failure mechanism for GDN layers: 1. The GDN metadata builder correctly classifies the step as a prefill (`num_prefills=1, num_spec_decodes=0`), **but** the persistent-buffer refresh in `GDNAttentionMetadataBuilder.build()` only happens in the spec/decode branches (gated on `num_prefills == 0`). A prefill build never touches the persistent buffers. 2. The FULL graph replays with **stale capture-time metadata**: `spec_state_indices_tensor` still holds `0 == NULL_BLOCK_ID` from `build_for_cudagraph_capture`. 3. The FLA kernels (`fused_recurrent`, `fused_sigmoid_gating`) and `causal_conv1d_update` all have null-block guards that **silently skip stores** when the state index is `NULL_BLOCK_ID` — correct padding hygiene, but here it swallows the entire prefill state write. 4. The request's conv/SSM states stay zero forever. The first sampled token already diverges; everything after is computed from a wrong recurrent state → deterministic garbage, and the drafter (whose own state is equally poisoned) gets ~0% acceptance. ## Measured evidence Same weights, same 3-token greedy prompt, per-block checksums of the GDN state pools after the prefill step (instrumented `execute_model` with `torch.cuda.synchronize`): | Config | state blocks written by the prefill | output | |---|---|---| | `PIECEWISE` (healthy) | `{1, 4, 7}` (target model, matching the request's block-table rows) + `{10}` (draft) | correct, deterministic | | `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` (bug) | **only `{10}`** (draft runs piecewise); target blocks stay all-zero | deterministic garbage from token 1 | Weight checksum identical in both boots; capture leaves the pools clean (all-zero before the first real step in both). Acceptance rate on mixed probes: 12% (bug) vs 79% (fixed/piecewise/eager). This also explains the confusing symptom pattern that made the bug look like a "speculative rejection/rollback corruption" (#40880-style reports): prompts that don't tokenize to exactly `1+k` tokens are dispatched normally and stay healthy, genuine uniform-decode FULL replays are correct (the spec branch does refresh persistent buffers), and the garbage is byte-identical across reboots because everything is deterministic. ## Reproduction vLLM 0.27.1 (logic identical on current main), Qwen3.5-MoE hybrid (30 GDN + 10 full-attn layers), 1 GPU: ```bash vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-MoE-FP8 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":2}' \ --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE"}' curl http://localhost:8000/v1/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{ "model": "...", "prompt": "中国的首都是", "max_tokens": 24, "temperature": 0}' # prompt must tokenize to exactly (1 + num_speculative_tokens) tokens; garbage output. # Same request with cudagraph_mode PIECEWISE or --enforce-eager → correct output. ``` Note the aliasing is generic: any batch of fresh `num_reqs` prompts scheduled as exactly `(1+k)` tokens each hits the same path, and `q_len==1` aliasing with 1-token prompts at `k=0` is possible in principle too. ## Suggested fix (verified locally) Uniform-decode classification should require every request in the batch to actually be **past its prompt**, not just match the shape: ```python def _is_uniform_decode(self, *, max_num_scheduled_tokens, uniform_decode_query_len, num_tokens, num_reqs, force_uniform_decode=None): if force_uniform_decode is not None: # keep capture-path bypass return force_uniform_decode if not (max_num_scheduled_tokens == uniform_decode_query_len and num_tokens == max_num_scheduled_tokens * num_reqs): return False ib = self.input_batch return bool((ib.num_computed_tokens_cpu[:num_reqs] >= ib.num_prompt_tokens[:num_reqs]).all()) ``` Aliased prefill batches then fall back to the PIECEWISE path (which is where prefills belong anyway); genuine uniform decodes keep the FULL graph. Verified on my deployment: garbage gone (byte-exact vs piecewise golden on the trap prompt), acceptance restored 12%→79%, no measurable perf regression (FULL graph retained for real decode batches; a 100k-context needle gate and short-decode throughput both match or beat the eager baseline). ## Related issues - #28015 — the inverse aliasing (uniform-decode batches mis-shaped by padding for MLA backends); same root class: shape-only dispatch classification. - #40880 / #40914 — Qwen3-Next hybrid × MTP × cudagraph degraded output; the fix merged there was TurboQuant-specific and this mechanism explains the remaining reports. - #34571, #39273, vllm-ascend#7148 — adjacent mamba/GDN spec-decode state-corruption reports. ## Environment vLLM 0.27.1 (bug verified byte-identical in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py` on current main), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 (Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration, 30 GDN + 10 full-attn), MTP k=2, fp8 KV, single ROCm gfx1151 GPU — the bug is in platform-independent dispatch logic (also reproduced with two different attention backends).
signals.author: allenzz-dev

signals.title: [Bug][KVOffload] PD Multi Tier discards parked KV after a fixed 60s, so a queued consumer recomputes
signals.text: ### Your current environment vLLM `main` (nightly `5a4c8d99`), plus #52912 applied. Two instances, prefill and decode, each running `OffloadingConnector` with `TieringOffloadingSpec` (CPU primary + `p2p` secondary tier). ### Describe the bug A PD Multi Tier producer discards stored KV 60 s after `submit_store` when no `FetchMsg` has bound the `kv_request_id` yet, so a consumer whose fetch is issued later finds nothing, burns its own 30 s load deadline, and recomputes the prompt. `_UNBOUND_STORE_TIMEOUT_S = 60.0` (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/manager.py`) is a fixed timer counted from store time. Nothing ties it to whether the consumer's request still exists or is merely queued behind other work, so the reap can fire while the request it belongs to is perfectly alive. When the late fetch arrives, the consumer waits out `_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S = 30.0` (`.../p2p/session/client.py`) before falling back to recompute. This is separate from #52808 and is not addressed by #52912; that fix makes a warm producer cascade its blocks, this is about how long those blocks survive while the peer has not asked for them yet. Reproduced with two vLLM instances and three curls - no router, no proxy, no scheduler involved. The only difference between the two cases is how long the consumer waits before fetching: | case | consumer fetch delay | consumer leg | bytes pulled | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | control | 5 s (inside the park) | 0.30 s | 580,962,816 | | late | 65 s (past the park) | 38.31 s | 0 | Producer log for the late case: ``` P2P <producer-ip>:7777: unbound store kv_request_id=park-late-39 timed out after 60s without a fetch - failing 1 job(s) ``` ### Why this fires in practice The 60 s clock does not start when prefill completes - it starts at the producer's FIRST stored chunk. `_build_store_jobs` iterates `scheduler_output.num_scheduled_tokens` (in-flight requests), `complete_store` cascades each finished store job to the secondary tiers every step, and `_reap_unbound_stores` keys off `batches[0].submitted_at`, the oldest batch, then pops the whole `kv_request_id`. Measured on an idle H200 with a 98 K-token producer leg: HTTP returned in 6.7 s, the first batch parked at +1 s, and with no fetch sent the reap fired at first-park + 60 s rather than completion + 60 s (the two predictions differ by 6 s in that setup; the log lands on the former). So the failing condition is not decoder queueing. The real budget is first-chunk-to-fetch < 60 s, where the fetch only happens after the remaining prefill, the producer's HTTP return, proxy dispatch, decode admission, and the decode scheduler's lookup/flush. The producer's own prefill spends the budget first: 6.7 s of it idle at 98 K tokens, 13.3 s under mild concurrent load on the same GPU. At real concurrency on long prompts the sum passes 60 s with the decoder never queueing at all. Each occurrence costs a 30 s stall plus a full prompt recompute, which feeds back into the load that caused the delay. Both leg-dispatch orders lose, so this cannot be fixed by the caller: - dispatch the legs concurrently and the fetch can arrive **before** the store, so demand parks and the consumer burns its 30 s deadline. This is what llm-d/llm-d-router#2451 fixes on the routing-proxy side, by running the prefill leg to completion before dispatching decode - dispatch them sequentially, as that PR does and as the NIXL path already did, and the fetch can arrive **after** the 60 s reap - this issue A post-reap fetch is also not rejected: the reap adds the id to `_failed_req_ids`, but the fetch-bind path never consults that set (it feeds only the consumer-side `lookup()` and dead-session teardown, despite the reap docstring saying otherwise). The late fetch binds, finds nothing, and parks silently until the consumer's 30 s deadline. ### Steps to reproduce Two instances, `PF` = producer, `DE` = consumer, both with the tiering spec and a `p2p` secondary tier. ```sh M=<model>; ID=park-$$ PROMPT=$(awk 'BEGIN{p="unique-'$ID' ";for(i=0;i<900;i++) p=p "alpha bravo charlie delta echo ";print p}') # producer leg: stores KV under ID, parks it (no peer has fetched yet) curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'producer http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \ -X POST "http://$PF:8000/v1/completions" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"model\":\"$M\",\"prompt\":\"$PROMPT\",\"max_tokens\":1,\"temperature\":0,\"kv_transfer_params\":{\"remote_decoder\":{\"kv_request_id\":\"$ID\"}}}" sleep 65 # 5 reproduces the working control curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'consumer http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \ -X POST "http://$DE:8200/v1/completions" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"model\":\"$M\",\"prompt\":\"$PROMPT\",\"max_tokens\":4,\"temperature\":0,\"kv_transfer_params\":{\"remote_prefiller\":{\"kv_request_id\":\"$ID\",\"remote_host\":\"$PF\",\"remote_port\":7777}}}" # watch vllm:kv_offload_load_bytes_total on the consumer across the pair ``` With `sleep 5` the consumer pulls the blocks in ~0.3 s. With `sleep 65` it transfers nothing and returns after ~38 s. ### The NIXL path already solves this `NixlConnector` faces the same question - how long does P hold blocks that D has not read yet - and answers it with a renewable lease rather than a fixed timer: - `_kv_lease_duration` (`nixl/base_scheduler.py`), default **30 s**, configurable via `kv_lease_duration` - `_heartbeat_interval = _kv_lease_duration // 6`, and D sends periodic lease-renewal heartbeats to P for every request it still intends to read - `decoder_kv_blocks_ttl`, default 480 s, for the client-driven turn-2 case So NIXL's nominal pin is *shorter* than the tier's 60 s, yet a queued consumer never loses its blocks: the lease is tied to consumer liveness, and only a consumer that has actually gone away lets it lapse. The p2p tier has no equivalent - no renewal, no way for the consumer to signal intent, and no config knob - so it cannot distinguish "the peer is still queued" from "the peer will never come". ### Suggested direction Tie the parked store's lifetime to the consumer's liveness instead of a fixed interval from store time. A few shapes that would work: - adopt the NIXL contract: let the consumer renew the parked store the way D renews P's lease, so a queued request keeps its KV and a dead one releases it promptly - failing that, let the consumer register intent for a `kv_request_id` before it is admitted, so the producer knows a peer is coming - at minimum make the interval configurable like `kv_lease_duration` is, since the right value depends on the deployment's admission latency Worth surfacing the reap as its own counter either way - today it is only a warning line, so operators see the consumer's recompute without the producer side that explains it. cc @liranschour

signals.title: vLLM v0.26.0: intermittent startup wedge — `shm_broadcast` block starvation kills rank 0 during `_initialize_kv_caches`, API stays up but generation is dead
signals.text: ## Summary On an 8-rank tensor-parallel deployment of GLM-5.2-FP8, vLLM v0.26.0 intermittently fails during engine start. ~60 s of shared-memory broadcast block starvation is followed by `RayWorkerProc rank=[0] died unexpectedly`, `RuntimeError: cancelled` from `shm_broadcast.acquire_read`, and `EngineDeadError`. **Observed in 5 of 7 startup attempts.** When a start does survive, the server is stable — one surviving instance served 40 consecutive authenticated generation requests over 2 hours with zero failures. So this is a startup-time race, not runtime decay. **Most damaging detail:** in 2 of 3 controlled trials the HTTP server still came up and answered `GET /v1/models` with 200 while generation was already dead. Any readiness check based on the models endpoint reports a healthy start for a wedged engine. Only an authenticated completion request detects it. ## Environment | | | |---|---| | vLLM | 0.26.0 | | Hardware | 8 × NVIDIA GB10, compute capability 12.1 (SM121), 128 GB unified LPDDR5X per node | | Driver / CUDA | 580.173.02 / 13.0 | | OS / kernel | Ubuntu 24.04.4, 6.17.0-1029-nvidia, aarch64 | | Model | `zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8` | | Executor | Ray, `distributed_executor_backend=ray` | | Topology | TP8, PP1, DP1, expert-parallel off, speculative decoding off | | Attention backend | `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120` | | KV cache dtype | `fp8_ds_mla` | | CUDA graph | `NONE` | | Interconnect | RoCEv2, dual 200 Gb/s ConnectX-7 rails, NCCL over IB | Serve arguments (constant across all trials): --tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 16384 --max-num-seqs 8 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.83 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8_ds_mla --attention-backend FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120 \ --enable-chunked-prefill --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"NONE"}' ## Observed sequence Timestamps from two independent trials. The starvation warning precedes the worker death by ~60 s in both, which suggests the block starvation is the primary event and the rank-0 death is downstream of it. Trial A: 13:11:01 INFO [shm_broadcast.py:705] No available shared memory broadcast block found in 60 seconds. This typically happens when some processes are hanging or doing some time-consuming work... 13:12:05 ERROR [ray_executor_v2.py:514] RayWorkerProc rank=[0] died unexpectedly, shutting down executor. 13:12:05 ERROR [core.py:1332] File ".../shm_broadcast.py", line 779, in dequeue 13:12:05 ERROR [core.py:1332] File ".../shm_broadcast.py", line 701, in acquire_read 13:12:05 ERROR [core.py:1332] RuntimeError: cancelled 13:12:05 ERROR [async_llm.py:704] vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError: EngineCore encountered an issue. Trial B (same signature, 59 s gap): 13:35:55 INFO [shm_broadcast.py:705] No available shared memory broadcast block found in 60 seconds 13:36:54 ERROR [ray_executor_v2.py:514] RayWorkerProc rank=[0] died unexpectedly 13:36:54 ERROR [core.py:1332] RuntimeError: cancelled 13:36:54 ERROR [async_llm.py:704] EngineDeadError Full call path captured on an earlier occurrence: core.py:136 __init__ -> core.py:324 _initialize_kv_caches -> abstract.py:124 initialize_from_config -> multiproc_executor.py:405 collective_rpc -> multiproc_executor.py:91 result -> multiproc_executor.py:95 _wait_for_response -> multiproc_executor.py:390 get_response -> mq.dequeue -> shm_broadcast.py:779 dequeue -> shm_broadcast.py:701 acquire_read -> RuntimeError("cancelled") The failure occurs inside `_initialize_kv_caches`, i.e. during the compilation / KV-config collective, before the model serves any request. ## Reproduction 1. Deploy `zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8` across 8 GB10 nodes with the arguments above. 2. Start the server; wait for the API to bind. 3. Issue an **authenticated completion** request (not `/v1/models`). 4. Repeat the full stop/start cycle. Roughly 5 of 7 cycles fail. Weight load is ~15 min per cycle, so failures are expensive to reproduce. ## Expected vs actual **Expected:** engine start either succeeds or fails loudly; a bound HTTP server implies a functional engine. **Actual:** the engine core dies during KV-cache initialisation, yet the API server can remain bound and answer `/v1/models` with 200. `POST /v1/completions` returns no tokens. A readiness probe on the models endpoint therefore reports success. ## What was ruled out - **Speculative decoding / MTP** — reproduced with MTP fully disabled. - **Context length** — reproduced at 16384 after 16384 had previously succeeded; also seen at 32768. - **Memory pressure** — no kernel OOM on any rank; engine reports 88.73 GiB weights, 1.4 GiB peak activation, 2.3 GiB non-torch against a 101.0 GiB budget, and separately advertises ~18 GiB of unused headroom. - **Interconnect** — NCCL reports `ncclCommInitRank ... Init COMPLETE` on all 8 ranks across both IB devices with ECE negotiated in ~2.3 s. Fabric counters show zero discards, zero retransmits and zero link events across the affected windows. - **KV dtype support** — `FlashInferMLASparseSM120Backend` declares `fp8_ds_mla` among its `supported_kv_cache_dtypes`. ## Patched-build isolation This runs on an image with local patches layered on v0.26.0, so the obvious question is whether those patches are implicated. They are not: **every file in the failure path is byte-identical between the patched build and an unpatched v0.26.0 build of the same base.** | file | unpatched | patched | |---|---|---| | `vllm/distributed/device_communicators/shm_broadcast.py` | `7ff67c2ef6b8a33a` | `7ff67c2ef6b8a33a` | | `vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py` | `fb279ff0e0a08681` | `fb279ff0e0a08681` | | `vllm/v1/engine/core.py` | `3ae1381a6af841e2` | `3ae1381a6af841e2` | | `vllm/v1/executor/abstract.py` | `419002195d13cf05` | `419002195d13cf05` | | `vllm/v1/executor/ray_executor_v2.py` | `5920e5924bd74b85` | `5920e5924bd74b85` | | `vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/flashinfer_mla_sparse.py` | `550079022e858952` | `550079022e858952` | | **aggregate of all `vllm/**/*.py`** | `af932612311083bf` | `8d3fa2ce4a73bcc0` | (sha256, first 16 hex chars.) The aggregate row differs, confirming the two images are genuinely distinct — the patches exist, they simply do not touch any module the traceback passes through. The local patch set targets speculative-decoding/MTP paths (`dsa_mtp_index_sharing`, `mtp_compact_shared_topk`, `glm52_mtp_indexer_correctness`), and this issue reproduces with **speculative decoding disabled**. ## Workaround Retry the start. Surviving instances are stable. At the observed rate this needs 3–4 attempts (~25 min each), which is not viable for production bring-up, so we have reverted to vLLM v0.23.0 with `TRITON_MLA_SPARSE` and `bfloat16` KV. That combination has started reliably every time. Note the cost of the workaround: v0.23.0's `TRITON_MLA_SPARSE` does not support any fp8 KV dtype, so reverting forfeits the `fp8_ds_mla` KV cache. Measured on identical context and utilisation, `fp8_ds_mla` on v0.26.0 gave **152,000 KV tokens / 9.28x max concurrency** versus **61,184 / 3.73x** on v0.23.0 — a 2.5x capacity difference. ## Suggested follow-up 1. `_initialize_kv_caches` appears to exceed the `shm_broadcast` block-acquisition window on slow multi-node startups. A longer or configurable timeout for the initialisation-phase collective may be sufficient. 2. Rank 0's own termination reason is not surfaced — the executor reports only "died unexpectedly". Propagating the worker's exit cause would make this diagnosable in one cycle rather than seven. 3. Consider having the API server refuse to bind, or report unready, when `EngineCore` has died, so that `/v1/models` cannot answer 200 for a dead engine. ## Evidence available Per-rank engine captures from 3 controlled trials (all 8 ranks each), full Ansible run logs, and fabric counter deltas across each window.

signals.title: [RFC]: Opt-out control for individual startup kernel warmups
signals.text: ### Motivation. `kernel_warmup()` (vllm/model_executor/warmup/kernel_warmup.py:98-215) runs a fixed warmup sequence from `Worker.compile_or_warm_up_model` (vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:728), just before CUDA graph capture. Per the module docstring (kernel_warmup.py:3-7) the sequence exists for JIT'ed kernels. Some entries are already individually controllable — `VLLM_DEEP_GEMM_WARMUP=skip` (:162-166), `kernel_config.enable_cutedsl_warmup` (:149), `kernel_config.enable_flashinfer_autotune` (:176-183) — and `kernel_config.enable_jit_warmup` (:110) is an all-or-nothing gate for the registry. But the set is ad hoc, and some entries have no switch at all: `qwen_triton_warmup` (:126) sits outside every gate. We maintain an out-of-tree hardware platform plugin for a non-CUDA accelerator, which redirects the GDN ops to an AOT-compiled kernel library. With no JIT to hide, the warmup is pure startup cost for us — and the dummy inputs upstream builds for the reference Triton kernels do not satisfy our AOT kernels' host-side argument validation. Concretely, `_warm_fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update_kernel` (vllm/model_executor/warmup/qwen_triton_warmup.py:203-241) builds `initial_state` as a rank-2 tensor (:216-220) and passes it at :235. The reference Triton path never notices, since it only reads `initial_state.stride(0)` (vllm/third_party/flash_linear_attention/ops/fused_sigmoid_gating.py:231) and forwards the tensor as a raw pointer (:253). Our kernel requires rank 4 and rejects it, so engine startup fails. ### Current workaround. Our plugin monkeypatches the private `qwen_triton_warmup._warm_fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update_kernel` into a no-op. It depends on a private symbol and breaks on any upstream refactor, which is what prompted this RFC. ### Proposed Change. One generic opt-out axis, rather than a new env var per warmup. Two sketches: **A — named warmups + skip list.** Give each entry in `kernel_warmup()` a stable name and add e.g. `VLLM_SKIP_KERNEL_WARMUPS=qwen_triton,deep_gemm`. This mirrors `VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS` (vllm/envs.py:1716-1724, consumed at kernel_warmup.py:218-234), which is already a comma-separated name skip list. **B — platform hook.** `current_platform.get_skip_kernel_warmups() -> set[str]`, consumed where `KernelConfig.set_platform_defaults` (vllm/config/kernel.py:285-311) already calls `current_platform.get_default_ir_op_priority` (vllm/platforms/interface.py:1299). A platform knows whether its kernels are JIT or AOT, so a plugin can declare this itself instead of asking operators to set env vars. The two compose: B supplies the default, A lets a user override it. Default behaviour is unchanged — an empty skip list or an unimplemented hook runs every warmup exactly as today. Purely additive and backward compatible. ### Feedback Period. _No response_ ### CC List. _No response_ ### Any Other Things. _No response_ ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signals.title: [Bug]: LoRA + Muse-Glimmer-30B: AssertionError in lora_shrink (token_lora_mapping.size(0) == M) at startup profiling, on stock nightly and regardless of adapter targets
signals.text: Enabling LoRA on Muse-Glimmer-30B kills the engine at startup, during the profiling dummy run, before any request is served. We hit this on our production fork first, then reproduced it on stock nightly in a fresh environment, so we ran a small discrimination matrix before reporting. All four cells fail on the same assert. **Failure:** ``` File ".../vllm/lora/ops/triton_ops/lora_shrink_op.py", in _lora_shrink assert token_lora_mapping.size(0) == M AssertionError EngineCore failed to start. ``` **Minimal repro:** ``` vllm serve bullerwins/Muse-Glimmer-30B-NVFP4 \ --quantization modelopt_fp4 --max-model-len 4096 --max-num-seqs 4 \ --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 8 \ --lora-modules probe=<rank-8 adapter> ``` The adapter content does not matter. Ours is a no-op probe (lora_B all zeros, rank 8, q/k/v/o + gate/up/down over the 52 text layers). Boot without `--enable-lora` is clean on the same checkpoint. **The matrix we ran (all four fail identically):** | stack | adapter targets | result | |---|---|---| | nightly `0.26.1rc1.dev1054+g6feafb8b7`, py3.12, torch 2.13.0+cu130, RTX 5090, fresh RunPod env | bare module names (`q_proj`, ...) | AssertionError | | same stock nightly, second fresh env | regex anchored to `model.language_model.layers...` (the pattern community adapters use) | AssertionError | | our fork (older base + local patches unrelated to LoRA), RTX 5090 | bare names | AssertionError | | our fork, `--enforce-eager` | anchored regex | AssertionError | The eager run rules out a compile or cudagraph interaction. Anchoring the target_modules to the language model, which is how every published Muse-Glimmer adapter on the Hub scopes its targets, changes nothing at boot time, so the failure is not about the adapter accidentally matching vision modules by name. **What looks relevant:** Muse-Glimmer is a multimodal ConditionalGeneration model, and this smells like a cousin of #26976 (visual encoder wrongly marked LoRA-enabled during profile_run, closed but per the last comments still biting qwen3-vl users on 0.11.0). The profile dummy run on this model includes vision tokens, and the LoRA token mapping length ends up desynchronized from M as lora_shrink sees it. For contrast, a hybrid but text-profiled model (Qwen3.5-9B, standard docker image) accepts the same style of no-op adapter without trouble on our side, which points at the multimodal profiling path rather than LoRA in general. Worth noting for whoever picks this up: as far as we can tell nobody currently serves Muse-Glimmer LoRA adapters through vLLM. The published adapters (lemuralabs, PursuitOfDataScience, sequelbox and others) all document transformers + peft on the bf16 base only. So this path may simply never have worked for this model. And if the startup assert gets fixed, #48862 (NVFP4 + LoRA illegal memory access on first request) is probably waiting right behind it for the quantized case. Happy to test patches, we have the repro down to a few minutes on a rented 5090. Full tracebacks from both stacks available on request.

signals.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4-Flash: non-deterministic output at temperature=0, rate scales with concurrency
signals.text:
### Your current environment ``` vLLM : 0.27.1 (installed from PyPI wheel, verified unmodified — all 4735 .py files hash-match the wheel) Model : nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-nvfp4-DSpark (NVFP4, DSpark draft head) GPU : NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC, 1x, TP=1 (compute capability 10.3) Driver : 580.126.09 torch : 2.13.0+cu132 (CUDA 13.2) OS : Ubuntu 24.04 ``` Serve command: ```bash vllm serve nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-nvfp4-DSpark \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.88 \ --max-model-len 1048576 --trust-remote-code --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 256 \ --max-num-seqs 256 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4 --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice --enable-prefix-caching \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}' \ --attention-config '{"use_fp4_indexer_cache":true}' \ --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE","custom_ops":["all"]}' \ --max-cudagraph-capture-size 128 ``` ### 🐛 Describe the bug **Summary:** with `temperature=0`, the same prompt returns **different completions** depending only on how many requests are in flight. Greedy decoding should be reproducible, so any variation is a bug. The rate rises with concurrency. #### Reproducer `repro.py` — sends the identical greedy request N times and counts distinct completions: ```python import concurrent.futures as cf, json, sys, time, urllib.request from collections import Counter URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions" MODEL = "nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-nvfp4-DSpark" IDS = [ "c_mhw9v76obuh72x98f4pb8xr3", "o_ftcj97ua0p5heapj5fpng02e", "c_3exww35axs739igmh42hvph1g", "c_8oold74tm25kw4uag86kyj16z", "c_6adnmt0f3gs4xfl4ne2x5zkjo", "c_z72re6iq4gltfujr1zrwll11y", "o_9klm2xr7ta4bnvq8wsdf31hgc", "c_pw4nz8tqm6ykxj02hcv5rb7ed", ] PROMPT = ("Echo each of these identifiers back to me, one per line, prefixed " "with 'ECHO: '. Do not modify any character. Do not add commentary.

" + "
".join(IDS)) BODY = {"model": MODEL, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}], "temperature": 0.0, "max_tokens": 2000} def call(_): req = urllib.request.Request(URL, data=json.dumps(BODY).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}) return json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=600).read() )["choices"][0]["message"]["content"] n, conc = int(sys.argv[1]), int(sys.argv[2]) if conc == 1: outs = [call(i) for i in range(n)] else: with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=conc) as ex: outs = [f.result() for f in cf.as_completed( [ex.submit(call, i) for i in range(n)])] v = Counter(outs) minority = sum(c for _, c in v.most_common()[1:]) print(f"n={len(outs)} conc={conc} DISTINCT={len(v)} " f"minority={minority} ({100*minority/len(outs):.2f}%)") print("EXPECTED at temperature=0: DISTINCT=1") ``` ```bash python repro.py 500 32 ``` #### Results — stock 0.27.1, 10/10 runs non-deterministic Each row is an independent run against the same server. | concurrency | n | runs | minority-output rate | |---|---|---|---| | 8 | 400 | 2 | 0.25%, 0.50% | | 16 | 400 | 3 | 2.25%, 1.75%, 1.75% | | 32 | 500 | 5 | 2.40%, 1.00%, 0.40%, 1.20%, 0.80% | `DISTINCT` was >1 in **every** run (up to 8 distinct completions in 500 requests). "minority" = responses differing from the modal completion. A typical divergence — one identifier comes back altered, the rest of the completion is byte-identical: ``` majority: ...ECHO: c_6adnmt0f3gs4xfl4ne2x5zkjo... variant : ...ECHO: o_9klm5t0f3gs4xfl4ne2x5zkjo... ``` #### This is not float non-determinism from reduction order Requesting `top_logprobs=20` at the divergent position: ``` conc=1 (correct): conc=32 (corrupt): '2' 0.000000 '5' -1.377942 'x' -18.375000 '7' -2.252942 '3' -20.250000 '6' -2.377942 '27' -21.125000 '8' -2.502942 '22' -21.125000 '4' -2.627942 ``` The correct arm is maximally confident: an **18-logprob** gap between top-1 and top-2 (~1e8 probability ratio). The corrupt arm collapses to a near-uniform distribution over digits, margin **0.1–2.0**. Batched-reduction float noise perturbs logits on the order of 1e-3 and could only flip a near-tie. Turning an 18-logprob margin into a coin flip means the **attention output feeding that position differs**, not that a tie broke the other way. The divergence also lands at a consistent token index across runs. #### Notes - Reproduced on **unmodified** 0.27.1 from PyPI (hash-verified against the wheel). - Also reproduces with `--enforce-eager` (4/5 runs non-deterministic), so it is not CUDA-graph capture/replay. - Not `seed`-related: at `temperature=0`, `SamplingParams.sampling_type` returns `GREEDY` before `seed` is consulted (`sampling_params.py`), and passing a seed changes nothing. - Requests were verified to complete successfully; runs with any transport error were discarded rather than counted. The flags above are the standard serving configuration for this model (sparse-MLA block size, fp8 KV cache, FP4 indexer cache, DSpark draft head). I have not isolated the mechanism and don't want to speculate. Happy to run further diagnostics on this hardware — e.g. with speculative decoding or prefix caching disabled, or with different `num_speculative_tokens` — if that helps.

signals.title: [Feature]: Cache-aware waiting QoS with optional cooperative prefill preemption
signals.text: #### Summary Add an opt-in V1 scheduling policy that improves time-to-first-token (TTFT) for cache-warm continuations under long-context contention: 1. **Cache-aware waiting admission/order**: within a bounded window, prefer a waiting request when its *estimated remaining service cost* is materially lower because a local or external KV prefix is already available. 2. **Optional cooperative prefill preemption (later phase)**: at an ordinary chunked-prefill scheduling boundary, checkpoint and pause a cold running prefill only when doing so is predicted to let a warm request reach its first streamed token significantly sooner, without losing the victim's completed work. This issue is intended to track one concrete policy/use case. It is compatible with the scheduler extension framework proposed in #51608 rather than a duplicate of that framework. #### Motivating workload A single engine may serve many concurrent, long-lived agent sessions with distinct 100k–500k-token histories. Under load, one or more uncached chunked prefills can occupy the running set while a continuation with hundreds of thousands of tokens already present in local APC or an external KV cache remains waiting. FCFS is fair by arrival time, but it can produce poor interactive latency in this case: the warm continuation may need only a cache transfer, a short uncached suffix, and one decode step, while a cold request ahead of it still has a very large prefill remaining. This is a QoS/tail-latency proposal, not a claim that cache affinity universally improves throughput. The corrected experiment reported in #42185 found no meaningful benefit for workloads sharing one already-resident prefix; multi-session workloads with distinct competing prefixes are the target case. #### Residency should be time-aware A large external-cache hit is not free: the cached prefix must still be loaded into GPU KV and resident while the request runs. However, that occupancy is temporal. For a warm request, the approximate active residence is: ``` cache load + uncached tail prefill + actual output tokens / effective per-request decode throughput ``` `max_tokens / effective_decode_tokens_per_second` is a useful upper bound for the decode portion (not multiplication); under mixed prefill/decode load, effective per-request decode throughput may be lower. Output KV pages are allocated progressively, while the loaded prompt prefix remains resident until completion or preemption. The admission objective should therefore consider **KV block-seconds**, not only instantaneous block count or cache-hit percentage. A huge warm prefix with a small output budget can still be an excellent latency trade: large compute avoidance, short expected residence. #### Phase 1: cache-aware waiting policy Implement an opt-in policy through #51608's future Score/QueueSort hooks, or initially as a narrowly scoped built-in scheduler policy: - Preserve explicit request priority as the outer ordering key. - Inspect only a bounded FCFS/priority-ordered candidate window. - Use side-effect-free, cycle-cached features. - Never perform connector RPC or blocking I/O in the scheduler hot path. - Consider an external hit only after the connector's asynchronous lookup has completed. - Keep deterministic tie-breaking. A candidate score should estimate TTFT improvement rather than rank raw hit tokens: ``` warm_ttft_cost = ready_cache_transfer_time(tier, bytes) + uncached_tokens / observed_prefill_rate + first_decode_step_cost residency_cost = required_prompt_blocks * predicted_active_seconds benefit = estimated_head_wait_avoided - warm_ttft_cost - admission/displacement cost - weighted_residency_cost ``` Useful read-only features: - local cached tokens; - external cached tokens, lookup readiness, and cache tier; - estimated transfer bytes/time; - uncached prompt remainder; - blocks required for admission; - prompt-prefill versus active-decode state; - waiting age, explicit priority, and optional tenant/SLA weight; - output-token budget as a conservative residence estimate. The KV connector API may need a side-effect-free snapshot such as: ```python CacheAdmissionInfo( ready: bool, matched_tokens: int, tier: CacheTier, estimated_load_bytes: int, estimated_load_seconds: float | None, ) ``` This API must not allocate/touch blocks, emit cache events, increment hit metrics, or start a transfer. Fairness and anti-thrash controls: - bounded candidate window; - maximum FCFS-head wait / aging deadline; - minimum predicted benefit and hysteresis; - per-session/tenant bypass budget; - do not bypass preempted recovery work indefinitely; - expose decision reasons without high-cardinality metric labels. #### Phase 2: cooperative cached preemption Queue reordering alone cannot admit a warm request when running prefixes occupy the required GPU KV. A later opt-in phase could reclaim a running **prefill** at an existing scheduler-step boundary. Required connector/scheduler contract: 1. Select only a prefill victim; protect active decodes, remote-KV loads, and near-finished prefills. 2. Identify the latest complete cache chunk common to every TP/PP rank. 3. Ensure that prefix is durable and reloadable before freeing its GPU blocks: - wait for store completion, or - pin the blocks until all-rank completion; - do not treat store submission as durability. 4. Requeue the victim with an explicit checkpoint token count. 5. Admit the warm request only if predicted benefit exceeds checkpoint/reload cost. 6. Reload the victim later; recompute only an incomplete tail. 7. On any connector timeout/failure, retain or safely recompute the victim rather than trusting partial external state. Suggested safeguards: - cooldown and maximum preemptions per request; - one cooperative preemption per scheduling cycle; - no preemption while connector store backlog/failure rate is elevated; - all-rank acknowledgement and failure injection tests; - no zero-progress preemption loops; - request cancellation and repeated-preemption coverage. #### Observability and evaluation Split waiting/deferred reasons sufficiently to distinguish cache lookup, KV load, capacity, grammar, and other constraints. Record: - candidate local/external hit and tier; - estimated versus actual load/prefill time; - scheduler decision reason; - prompt blocks and predicted/actual block-seconds; - checkpointed tokens and store-fence latency; - reload tokens/time and recomputed tail; - TTFT/time-to-first-stream won or lost; - preemption count, cooldown rejection, and fairness age. Acceptance criteria: - default FCFS and priority behavior is unchanged when disabled; - scheduler hot path performs no external I/O; - deterministic unit tests for bounded reorder, aging, explicit priority, and starvation; - connector tests for delayed/failed all-rank checkpoint and immediate block-ID reuse; - A/B traces with multiple distinct long-context sessions; - report scheduler CPU overhead, p50/p95/p99 TTFT, time-to-first-stream, throughput, cache transfer bandwidth, GPU-KV churn, and fairness. ### Alternatives - **Existing integer priority**: useful for explicit interactive/batch QoS, but it does not estimate cache reuse or residency cost and currently has limited ability to displace running work (#40004, #40087). - **Smaller prefill chunks / lower `max_num_batched_tokens`**: creates more frequent scheduling boundaries but does not reclaim GPU KV and can reduce aggregate prefill throughput. - **Session affinity only**: #51384 is a safer and useful local-APC specialization, but external-cache readiness/tier and residency cost remain unmodeled. - **Residual SJF only**: #51375 captures remaining local work and aging, but does not incorporate external connector transfer cost. - **External proxy/router**: lacks exact per-engine KV allocation, cache readiness, and preemption state. - **Whole scheduler subclass**: possible through `scheduler_cls`, but unnecessarily couples a policy experiment to the full scheduler compatibility surface. - **Separate engines for interactive and batch traffic**: provides isolation but can strand GPU capacity and duplicates large model residency. ### Additional context Prior art and adjacent work: - #51608 — extensible scheduler Score/Filter/QueueSort/Preemption hooks. - #51384 — bounded session-affinity scheduler with local cache confirmation and aging. - #51375 — residual-aware SJF with aging. - #42185 — cache-affinity scheduling experiment and workload-dependent result. - #7883 / #10128 — prefix-cache-aware capacity and token-budget accounting. - #40004 / #40087 — waiting priority and running-request preemption. - #31731 / #36390 — KV-heavy head-of-line blocking. - #30256 — SLA-tiered scheduling. - LMCache/LMCache#4612 — reload already-cached KV for MP preempted requests. - vLLM #52360 / #52372 — precedent showing that async stores must not read freed/reused paged-KV blocks. A staged implementation is important: **waiting-order affinity should land and be measured independently; forced cooperative preemption should remain disabled until durable checkpoint/reload semantics are proven.** ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Searched existing and past issues/PRs and reviewed the related proposals above.

signals.title: [Bug]: `--reasoning-parser qwen3` returns the whole answer as `reasoning` (content=null) when the prompt already closes the think block but `enable_thinking` was not passed via chat_template_kwargs
signals.text:
### Your current environment Code-level report against vLLM `main` at `5ee84d3c` (2026-08-21); the files cited below are unchanged on `main` at `2740c817` (time of writing). I traced the serving/parser code and rendered the prompts through the `transformers` Jinja environment; I did not run a GPU server myself. The runtime symptom was reproduced by a third party on `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8` with vLLM `311b3513` (`--chat-template` + `--reasoning-parser qwen3`, non-streaming): https://huggingface.co/froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates/discussions/74. No `collect_env.py` output for that reason. ### 🐛 Describe the bug **Symptom.** With `--reasoning-parser qwen3`, a request whose rendered prompt already ends with a *closed* think block ``` <|im_start|>assistant <think> </think> ``` (i.e. thinking disabled by the chat template) but where `chat_template_kwargs["enable_thinking"]` was **not** set to `false`, gets its whole answer returned as `message.reasoning` with `content: null`. With `include_reasoning=false` the answer disappears. When does a template close the think block without `enable_thinking=false`? Whenever it supports another switch. The widely used community template for Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 (`froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates`) does this for `chat_template_kwargs: {"reasoning_effort": "none"}`, for an inline `<|think_off|>` tag in the user message, and for `auto_disable_thinking_with_tools=true`. The parser only sees `enable_thinking`, so template and parser disagree (same family as #43728, different trigger). **Root cause (code trace).** 1. `Qwen3Parser.__init__` sets `self.thinking_enabled = chat_kwargs.get("enable_thinking", True)` and builds the engine config with `initial_state = REASONING` from it (`vllm/parser/qwen3.py:225-236`). Nothing inspects the prompt. `adjust_initial_state_from_prompt` is the base no-op (`vllm/parser/engine/parser_engine.py:185`). Gemma4 overrides it for the mirror case (prompt ends *inside* an open reasoning block → start in `REASONING`, `vllm/parser/gemma4.py:508`, #45834); Qwen3 has no override for "prompt ends with a *closed* block → start in `CONTENT`". 2. The engine starts in `REASONING`; the model never emits `</think>` (the template already closed it), so every token becomes a `REASONING_CHUNK`, and `finish()` only appends `REASONING_END` (`vllm/parser/engine/streaming_parser_engine.py:313-317`; non-streaming assembly in `vllm/parser/engine/parser_engine.py:493-518`). Result: `reasoning=<the answer>`, `content=None`. 3. Which request paths are affected: - `--reasoning-parser qwen3` **plus** `--tool-call-parser qwen3_xml` / `qwen3_coder` (the recommended Qwen3.x config): `ParserManager.get_parser` returns the `Qwen3Parser` engine itself because both adapters share the engine class (`vllm/parser/parser_manager.py:141-143`). Then **both** streaming (`ParserEngine.parse_delta`, `parser_engine.py:430`, prompt hook is the no-op) and non-streaming (`ParserEngine.parse`, `parser_engine.py:665`) misroute. - `--reasoning-parser qwen3` alone (DelegatingParser): streaming is correct, because `Parser.parse_delta` checks `is_reasoning_end(prompt_token_ids)` before the first delta (`vllm/parser/abstract_parser.py:817-826`) and `</think>` is a single token (248069 in the Qwen3.x vocab). Non-streaming still misroutes: `Parser.parse` → `extract_reasoning` never sees the prompt (`abstract_parser.py:789-797`). 4. The serving layer already computes the right answer: `reasoning_ended = parser.is_reasoning_end(prompt_token_ids or [])` at `vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/serving.py:348` is `True` for this prompt, but it is only handed to the engine for structured outputs, not used by the output parser. Channels that *do* work today, for reference: `chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false}` and the top-level `reasoning_effort: "none"` (which `build_chat_params` turns into `enable_thinking=false`, `chat_completion/protocol.py:587-588`). **Minimal reproduction (expected from the trace; not run by me).** A two-line template that always prefills the closed think block isolates the parser from any template kwarg: ```jinja {%- for m in messages %}{{ '<|im_start|>' + m.role + '
' + m.content + '<|im_end|>
' }}{%- endfor %} {%- if add_generation_prompt %}{{ '<|im_start|>assistant
<think>

</think>

' }}{%- endif %} ``` ```bash vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B --chat-template closed_think.jinja \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"model":"Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 2+2?"}]}' ``` Expected: `"content": "4"`, `"reasoning": null`. Actual (per the trace and the third-party report): `"reasoning": "4"`, `"content": null`. Same for `"stream": true` in this config. Any Qwen3-family model works for the test; the `<think>`/`</think>` tokens are in all their vocabularies. **Suggested fix.** 1. Give `Qwen3Parser` an `adjust_initial_state_from_prompt` override (mirror of Gemma4's): if the last think marker in `prompt_token_ids` is `</think>` (the existing `is_reasoning_end` semantics — a thinking-on prompt ends with an open `<think>
`, so it stays `False` there even with preserved history), reset the engine to `CONTENT` and mark reasoning ended. That fixes the engine streaming path. 2. For non-streaming, pass `prompt_token_ids` (already available as `final_res.prompt_token_ids`) or the `reasoning_ended` value from `serving.py:348` into `parser.parse(...)` so `ParserEngine.parse` / `Parser.parse` can start in `CONTENT`. That also fixes the DelegatingParser non-streaming path generically. Related: #43728 (template/parser kwarg mismatch → `content: null`), #49717 / #45834 (Gemma4, opposite polarity). ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signals.title: [New Model]: TR-HASH deterministic token-routed MoE
signals.text: ## The model to consider - Model: https://huggingface.co/AETHORIA-AI/TR-HASH-MoE-200M-160B-SFT - Reference implementation: https://github.com/Complexity-ML/complexity-framework - Current serving engine: https://github.com/Complexity-ML/TR-Hash-i64 - License: Apache-2.0 for the SFT checkpoint TR-HASH is a 201.2M-parameter decoder-only causal language model with 16 layers, GQA, tied embeddings, four stored experts, top-2 activation, and an always-on shared SwiGLU path. Unlike conventional sparse MoE models, expert selection is not produced by a learned router. It is a deterministic function of token IDs, the layer index, and persisted multi-hash routing tables. ## The closest model vLLM already supports Mixtral is the closest execution shape because it combines a decoder-only transformer with top-k sparse experts: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/models/mixtral.py Llama is also relevant for the surrounding decoder/GQA structure. However, neither model has TR-HASH's deterministic token-ID routing or its stacked expert-weight representation. ## What's the difficulty of supporting this model? The principal differences are: 1. The MLP needs token IDs in addition to hidden states so that each layer can look up deterministic expert routes. 2. Routing tables are persisted integer buffers and must remain paired with the expert weights. 3. Routed projections are stored as stacked tensors rather than separate Linear modules: - `expert_gate`: `[num_experts, hidden_size, expert_width]` - `expert_up`: `[num_experts, hidden_size, expert_width]` - `expert_down`: `[num_experts, expert_width, hidden_size]` 4. A shared SwiGLU path is always active alongside the top-2 routed experts. 5. The public checkpoint currently uses custom framework configuration and weights. A full Hugging Face `AutoModelForCausalLM` adapter is planned but is not yet complete. The core implementation is here: - Engine: https://github.com/Complexity-ML/complexity-framework/blob/main/complexity/tr_hash/engine.py - MLP adapter: https://github.com/Complexity-ML/complexity-framework/blob/main/complexity/core/mlp/tr_hash_engine.py vLLM's Transformers backend documentation notes that custom MoE blocks should expose an `experts` attribute. We would appreciate guidance on whether TR-HASH should first target that backend through a Transformers-compatible adapter or whether the deterministic routing contract warrants a native vLLM model implementation. ## Motivation We want a standard high-throughput serving path for this open model and a deployment target for low-bit checkpoints produced through Intel AutoRound. The immediate integration chain is: `TR-HASH Hugging Face checkpoint -> AutoRound W4A16 -> vLLM serving -> Intel Low-Bit Open LLM Leaderboard` Intel leaderboard: https://huggingface.co/spaces/Intel/low_bit_open_llm_leaderboard AutoRound model support is being requested separately because its current Linear-oriented quantization path does not directly cover TR-HASH's stacked 3D expert tensors. ## Definition of done Support would be complete when: 1. vLLM can load the public TR-HASH checkpoint. 2. Deterministic routing tables remain unchanged and expert selection matches the reference implementation. 3. Fixed-prompt logits match the reference PyTorch implementation within an agreed tolerance. 4. Greedy generation produces the same token sequence for a small regression panel. 5. The model can be served through vLLM's OpenAI-compatible API. 6. The integration has a documented path for a future AutoRound W4A16 checkpoint. We are the model authors and can provide reference logits, routing traces, small test fixtures, and help with an implementation or PR.

signals.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4-Flash crashes at startup on 8x H20 (SM90) with v0.27.1 — Engine core initialization failed
signals.text: ### Environment - **GPU**: 8x NVIDIA H20 (SM90 / Hopper), single node - **Driver**: 575.57.08 (CUDA 12.9) - **vLLM**: `v0.27.1-cu129` (also reproduced with `v0.27.1` / CUDA 13.0.2) - **Model**: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` (UE8M0 FP8) - **Tensor parallel**: 8 ### Launch command (relevant flags) ``` --model /data/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 --served-model-name deepseek-v4-flash --tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 1000000 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 256 --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4 --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"greedy"}' ``` ### What happens `v0.25.0` starts fine. After upgrading to `v0.27.1`, startup crashes in two stages: **Stage 1** — `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` raised from `c10d::symmetric_memory::CUDASymmetricMemory` (same as #25937). Fixed by setting `TORCH_SYMM_MEM_DISABLE_MULTICAST=1`. **Stage 2** (after applying the fix above) — the model loads successfully, but a worker crashes during TileLang MLA/MHC kernel warmup, and the APIServer then exits with: ``` RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. Failed core proc(s): {} ``` Setting `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=1800` does **not** help (the raise is triggered by a core proc exiting, not a timeout). ### Logs ``` (Worker_TP0) INFO ... TileLang begins to compile kernel `mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm_tilelang` (Worker_TP0) INFO ... TileLang completes to compile kernel `mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm_tilelang` (EngineCore) INFO ... No available shared memory broadcast block found in 60 seconds. This typically happens when some processes are hanging or doing some time-consuming work (e.g. compilation, weight/kv cache quantization). ... (APIServer) RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. Failed core proc(s): {} ``` ### Related - #25937 — symmetric memory rendezvous crash on TP=8 (stage 1, confirmed). - For stage 2 (worker crash during TileLang `mhc_*_tilelang` warmup), likely candidates: - #51972 — SM90 (Hopper) cudagraph capture OOB read (`compress_ratio=4` → all-zero seq_lens), still Open. Caveat: our deployment auto-enables **breakable** cudagraph and we did NOT see "Capturing CUDA graphs (decode, FULL)", so it may not be the exact same bug. - #53055 — guard DeepGEMM in MHC pre-broadcast; closely matches our `mhc_*_tilelang` kernels. - Note: #49268/#49306 (MLA head dims read as zero) was merged Jul 21, so likely already in v0.27.1 — probably NOT our root cause. ### Note This is on **SM90 (H20)**, so it is not the DeepGEMM SM120/SM121 scale-factor regression (#52035).

signals.title: [Bug]: [ROCm][Spec Decode]  DFlash2 acceptance length collapses with default ROCM_ATTN draft backend
signals.text: ### Your current environment ## Summary DFlash2 with `ROCM_ATTN` draft attention has normal greedy acceptance with one request in flight, but acceptance collapses when requests are batched. Changing only the draft backend to `TRITON_ATTN` restores stable acceptance and more than doubles throughput at concurrency 4. The issue also reproduces with `--enforce-eager`. Preventing the ROCm prefix-attention kernel from loading evicted sliding-window K/V restores acceptance and throughput. ## Environment - GPU: 1x AMD MI350X (`gfx950`), TP=1 - ROCm/HIP: 7.1 (`7.1.52802`) - PyTorch: `2.11.0+rocm7.1` - vLLM: `0.26.1rc1.dev1045+g3406ec1da` - Commit: `3406ec1dae9916f920b90f0dbf90dcf54923d042` - PR: #52816 - AITER: `amd-aiter==0.1.0` - Target model: Qwen3.8-27B - Draft model: `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` - Target attention: `ROCM_AITER_FA` - Draft tokens: 7 - Prefix caching: disabled - Async scheduling: enabled - Hybrid cache attention block size: 832 tokens ### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Reproduction ```bash export HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 vllm serve /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B \ --served-model-name Qwen3.8-27B-VLLM-DFLASH2-ROCM \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8006 \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 65536 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --async-scheduling \ --generation-config vllm \ --attention-backend ROCM_AITER_FA \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":7,"attention_backend":"ROCM_ATTN"}' \ --trust-remote-code ``` ```bash vllm bench serve \ --backend vllm \ --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8006 \ --model /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B \ --served-model-name Qwen3.8-27B-VLLM-DFLASH2-ROCM \ --dataset-name random \ --random-input-len 5000 \ --random-output-len 256 \ --random-range-ratio 0 \ --num-prompts 64 \ --request-rate inf \ --max-concurrency 4 \ --ignore-eos \ --temperature 0 \ --seed 12 ``` Repeat with `--max-concurrency 1`. For the control, change only the draft `attention_backend` from `ROCM_ATTN` to `TRITON_ATTN`. ## Results | Draft backend | Concurrency | Output tok/s | TTFT | TPOT | Accepted length | Acceptance | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | ROCM_ATTN | 1 | 172.34 | 336.72 ms | 4.50 ms | 5.08 | 58.29% | | TRITON_ATTN | 1 | 192.18 | 334.38 ms | 3.91 ms | 5.09 | 58.44% | | ROCM_ATTN | 4 | 184.17 | 524.09 ms | 19.72 ms | 1.47 | 6.76% | | TRITON_ATTN | 4 | 421.06 | 526.14 ms | 7.33 ms | 4.99 | 57.05% | | ROCM_ATTN + `--enforce-eager` | 4 | 107.96 | 645.06 ms | 34.28 ms | 1.88 | 12.60% | An earlier independent ROCm concurrency-4 run also failed: 209.38 output tok/s, accepted length 1.77, and 11.07% acceptance. During a failing run, the server reported: ```text SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.03, Accepted: 39 tokens, Drafted: 9548 tokens, Per-position acceptance rate: 0.008, 0.005, 0.004, 0.003, 0.003, 0.003, 0.003, Avg Draft acceptance rate: 0.4% ``` ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

signals.title: TurboQuant KV cache: two observations from an sm121 evaluation: hybrid-model init failure; fp16 zero-point overflow on large value outliers
signals.text: (hybrid-model init failure; fp16 zero-point overflow on large value outliers)** We evaluated the TurboQuant KV-cache presets on a GB10 (sm121) against our production NVFP4-KV recipe and hit two things worth reporting. Full probe code, raw results, and methodology are public.¹ **1. Hybrid linear-attention models fail at engine init.** `--kv-cache-dtype turboquant_4bit_nc` with a hybrid model (GDN linear-attention layers alongside full-attention layers) fails with: ``` ValueError: Unknown TurboQuant cache dtype: 'auto'. Valid presets: turboquant_k8v4, turboquant_4bit_nc, turboquant_k3v4_nc, turboquant_3bit_nc ``` The state layers resolve to cache dtype `auto`, and the TurboQuant backend has no path for a mixed-layer model. If hybrids are intended to be unsupported, a clearer message ("hybrid models unsupported") at config-validation time would fail earlier and clearer; if support is intended, this is the blocker. Happy to test either on sm121. **2. The value path's fp16 zero-point silently overflows on large outliers (probe-level).** `triton_turboquant_store` keeps the per-vector value scale and zero-point in fp16 regardless of input dtype (`sc_f16` / `zr_f16`). With bf16 inputs containing an attention-sink-scale outlier of |min| > 65504, the zero-point overflows and the reconstructed values come back as **∞** — a poisoned cache line rather than graceful degradation. We verified this in a model-free store→decode round-trip (single-key decode isolates the value path): at a measured-provenance sink of ~125k the reconstruction is ∞ for every preset; at ~42k it is finite (outliers exact, at the cost of a coarser step for the rest of that token's vector — expected per-vector-scale behavior). Values of this magnitude do occur in real checkpoints (we measured v-cache sinks up to ~125k on a current 27B). A possible mitigation: store scale/zero in fp32 (+4 bytes per vector) or clamp with a warning. We could not confirm the overflow end to end on our model family because of observation 1 — so this stands as a kernel-level finding with a deterministic repro. Repro probe (self-contained, no model needed): https://github.com/TechPrototyper/local-ai-lab/blob/master/probes/turboquant_vs_nvfp4_value_probe.py ¹ https://github.com/TechPrototyper/local-ai-lab/blob/master/notes/turboquant-vs-nvfp4-kv-value-probe.md

signals.title: [Bug]: _fwd_kernel_ep_scatter_2 ignores recv_x_scale_stride1 for column-major f32 scales when num_tokens >= 2
signals.text: ## Environment - vLLM nightly `0.26.1rc1.dev926+gb05ae5dc0` (collect_env output attached below attached below); bug present in current `main` source of `deep_gemm_utils.py`. - Hardware: 2× RTX 5090 (SM120), TP=2, CUDA 12.x. - Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 (DeepGEMM grouped-FP8 contiguous MoE path). <details> <summary>collect_env output</summary> ``` Collecting environment information... uv is set ============================== System Info ============================== OS : Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (x86_64) GCC version : (Ubuntu 15.2.0-16ubuntu1) 15.2.0 Clang version : Could not collect CMake version : version 3.31.6 Libc version : glibc-2.43 ============================== PyTorch Info ============================== PyTorch version : 2.13.0+cu130 Is debug build : False CUDA used to build PyTorch : 13.0 ROCM used to build PyTorch : N/A XPU used to build PyTorch : N/A ============================== Python Environment ============================== Python version : 3.12.13 (main, Jul 18 2026, 17:02:19) [Clang 22.1.3 ] (64-bit runtime) Python platform : Linux-7.0.0-29-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.43 ============================== CUDA / GPU Info ============================== Is CUDA available : True CUDA runtime version : Could not collect CUDA_MODULE_LOADING set to : GPU models and configuration : GPU 0: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU 1: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 Nvidia driver version : Could not collect cuDNN version : Could not collect HIP runtime version : N/A MIOpen runtime version : N/A ``` </details> ## Summary In the non-`PACK_UE8M0` (f32-scales) branch of `_fwd_kernel_ep_scatter_2` (`vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/deep_gemm_utils.py`), the scale row is loaded as: ```python to_copy_s = tl.load( recv_x_scale + token_id * recv_x_scale_stride0 + offset_in_s, mask=mask_s, ) ``` `offset_in_s` (the group index) is added **without multiplying by `recv_x_scale_stride1`**, although the kernel receives that stride and uses it correctly in the `PACK_UE8M0` branch (`g0 * recv_x_scale_stride1`, …). The f32 branch therefore assumes a row-major scale tensor (`stride1 == 1`). ## Impact `per_token_group_quant_fp8(..., column_major_scales=True)` — the MoE-input quant used on this path — returns scales with strides `(1, num_tokens)`. At `num_tokens == 1` the layout coincides with row-major and the read is accidentally correct. At `num_tokens >= 2` the kernel reads address `token_id + g` instead of `token_id + g * num_tokens`, so each scattered row receives scales from the wrong token/group coordinates — other tokens' group scales are copied into the expert-workspace scale rows that the grouped GEMM then consumes. In our random synthetic fixtures the mis-association was numerically masked (max end-output delta ~1e-9, because adjacent groups of a token frequently share a power-of-two scale), which makes the bug easy to miss in tolerance-based tests; deterministic constructions with distinct per-token magnitudes expose it immediately. ## Reproducible example ```python import torch from vllm.model_executor.layers.quantization.utils.fp8_utils import ( per_token_group_quant_fp8) from vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe.deep_gemm_utils import ( deepgemm_moe_permute) c, H, E, topk = 2, 2048, 256, 8 dev = "cuda" x = torch.zeros(c, H, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=dev) # token t, group g -> distinct per-token magnitude bands so every # (t, g) has a unique power-of-two exponent for t in range(c): for g in range(16): x[t, g * 128:(g + 1) * 128] = 2.0 ** (g - 8 + 20 * t) topk_ids = torch.arange(c * topk, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev).reshape(c, topk) % E xq, xs = per_token_group_quant_fp8( x, 128, column_major_scales=True, use_ue8m0=True) aq_out, aq_scale_out, m_indices, inv_perm, _ = deepgemm_moe_permute( aq=xq, aq_scale=xs, topk_ids=topk_ids, local_num_experts=E, expert_map=None, expert_tokens_meta=None) # expected: the scale row scattered to each routed (t, k) destination # equals the source token's quant scales for t in range(c): for k in range(topk): dest = int(inv_perm[t, k]) got = aq_scale_out[dest] # f32, [M_sum, 16] exp = xs[t] # logical [16], col-major if not torch.equal(got.cpu(), exp.float().cpu()): print(f"MISASSOCIATED at t={t} k={k}: " f"got exponents {torch.log2(got).tolist()} != " f"expected {torch.log2(exp.float()).tolist()}") raise SystemExit(1) print("all scale rows correct (bug not reproduced on this build)") ``` Observed (nightly above, `c=2`): every routed row fails — e.g. for a source token whose true group-7 exponent is the odd one out, the scattered row carries it at group 14, exactly the `t + g` addressing (with strides `(1, 2)`, `t + g` for `g=7` aliases `t=1, g_true=7` storage position of `t + 2*7`). Expected: bitwise-equal rows as the assertion demands. At `c=1` the script passes (layout coincidence). ## Suggested fix Mirror the packed branch — multiply the group offset by the stride: ```python to_copy_s = tl.load( recv_x_scale + token_id * recv_x_scale_stride0 + offset_in_s * recv_x_scale_stride1, mask=mask_s) ``` No signature change (the stride is already an argument). Regression test: the script above at `num_tokens in (1, 2, 4)`. Found while developing a standalone fused-prepare prototype for this path. Happy to send a PR with the fix + regression test. --- *Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the reporter; the diagnosis and reported hardware observations were verified by the reporter.*

signals.title: [Bug]: UE8M0 per_token_group_quant_fp8 scales differ between the C++ and Triton fallback paths for tiny groups
signals.text: ## Environment - vLLM nightly `0.26.1rc1.dev926+gb05ae5dc0` (collect_env output attached below attached below); divergence verified bitwise on hardware below; both implementations checked against current `main` (`fp8_utils.py` Triton fallback; `csrc/libtorch_stable/ quantization/w8a8/fp8/per_token_group_quant.cu`). - Hardware: 2× RTX 5090 (SM120), CUDA 12.x. - Path: `per_token_group_quant_fp8` in `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/fp8_utils.py`. The CUDA/contiguous dispatch runs the C++ op (`torch.ops._C.per_token_group_fp8_quant`); other inputs (e.g. non-contiguous) run the in-file Triton fallback. <details> <summary>collect_env output</summary> ``` Collecting environment information... uv is set ============================== System Info ============================== OS : Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (x86_64) GCC version : (Ubuntu 15.2.0-16ubuntu1) 15.2.0 Clang version : Could not collect CMake version : version 3.31.6 Libc version : glibc-2.43 ============================== PyTorch Info ============================== PyTorch version : 2.13.0+cu130 Is debug build : False CUDA used to build PyTorch : 13.0 ROCM used to build PyTorch : N/A XPU used to build PyTorch : N/A ============================== Python Environment ============================== Python version : 3.12.13 (main, Jul 18 2026, 17:02:19) [Clang 22.1.3 ] (64-bit runtime) Python platform : Linux-7.0.0-29-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.43 ============================== CUDA / GPU Info ============================== Is CUDA available : True CUDA runtime version : Could not collect CUDA_MODULE_LOADING set to : GPU models and configuration : GPU 0: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU 1: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 Nvidia driver version : Could not collect cuDNN version : Could not collect HIP runtime version : N/A MIOpen runtime version : N/A ``` </details> ## Summary — scope: `use_ue8m0=True` only With UE8M0 scales enabled, the two implementations of the same op apply different floors and produce different scales for tiny groups: - **C++ kernel** floors twice: `absmax` by the passed `eps`, then — in the UE8M0 branch — the scale by a **hard-coded `1e-10`** before `ceil_pow2`: ```text local_absmax = max(absmax, eps) scale = ceil_pow2(max(local_absmax / fp8_max, 1e-10)) ``` For an all-zero group (default eps): scale = `2^-33` (measured bitwise: scattered f32 scale rows read exactly `1.1641532182693481e-10`). - **Triton fallback** floors only the absmax: ```python _absmax = tl.maximum(tl.max(tl.abs(y)), eps) scale_raw = _absmax * (1.0 / fp8_max) y_s = tl.math.exp2(tl.ceil(tl.log2(scale_raw))) # ue8m0 ``` For the same zero group: `ceil(log2(1e-10/448)) = -42` → `2^-42 ≈ 2.27e-13` — a **smaller (finer) scale** than the C++ path's coarser `2^-33` floor. Consequently, for groups whose absmax is small enough (see thresholds), the two paths emit different UE8M0 scales and different fp8 codes for tiny-but-nonzero values. With `use_ue8m0=False` both paths compute the same non-UE8M0 scale and no divergence exists. ## Thresholds (both stated to avoid confusion) - Pre-rounding floor boundary: `absmax/448 < 1e-10`, i.e. `absmax < 4.48e-8`, is where the C++ hard floor engages. - Because UE8M0 scales round up to a power of two, the **observable** divergence window is narrower: the fallback first agrees with the C++ `2^-33` once `absmax > 448 · 2^-34 ≈ 2.61e-8`. Between ~2.61e-8 and 4.48e-8 both round to the same scale; below ~2.61e-8 they differ (down to `2^-42` at and near zero). ## Reproducible example ```python import torch from vllm.model_executor.layers.quantization.utils.fp8_utils import ( per_token_group_quant_fp8) # non-contiguous rows force the Triton fallback (dispatch checks # x.is_contiguous()); a padded-row slice is reliably non-contiguous x_fb = torch.zeros(2, 2049, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")[:, :2048] assert not x_fb.is_contiguous() x_fb[:, 0] = 1e-12 # tiny-but-nonzero member of group 0 x_cpp = x_fb.contiguous() q_cpp, s_cpp = per_token_group_quant_fp8(x_cpp, 128, use_ue8m0=True) q_fb, s_fb = per_token_group_quant_fp8(x_fb, 128, use_ue8m0=True) print(torch.log2(s_cpp.float()[0]), torch.log2(s_fb.float()[0])) ``` Observed (environment above): C++ scale exponent `-33` vs fallback `-42`, and the fp8 code for the `1e-12` element differs between paths. (For reference, an input of `1e-9` shows `-33` vs ~`-38` — the gap shrinks as magnitudes grow toward the `2.61e-8` crossover.) ## Impact Narrow but real: the two implementations of the same op disagree under UE8M0, which matters for (a) bit-parity between configurations that dispatch differently (contiguous vs not), (b) anything consuming scales directly (UE8M0 packing), and (c) exact-parity test suites. Found while writing a bitwise-exact reimplementation of this op; matching the C++ scale-floor semantics was required for bitwise parity with production, and the fallback's different floor was confirmed against source. ## Suggested fix Align the Triton fallback to the C++ semantics, **conditionally on `use_ue8m0`** (an unconditional change would create a new non-UE8M0 divergence): ```python scale_raw = _absmax * (1.0 / fp8_max) if use_ue8m0: scale_raw = tl.maximum(scale_raw, 1e-10) y_s = tl.math.exp2(tl.ceil(tl.log2(scale_raw))) if use_ue8m0 \ else scale_raw ``` applied to **both** fallback kernels in the file (row-major and column-major variants), with regression tests covering both layouts and both `use_ue8m0` settings at zero and sub-threshold magnitudes. ## Why align to the C++ kernel (and not the reverse) 1. **Zero risk to primary-path numerics.** The C++ op serves the overwhelming majority of real traffic (contiguous CUDA inputs); redefining ITS semantics would change shipped behavior for everyone to fix a corner case — the opposite trade a parity fix should make. Aligning the rarely-executed fallback changes behavior only for configurations that currently disagree with the main path anyway. 2. **The C++ double floor reads as deliberate.** The UE8M0 branch applies an explicit hard-coded scale floor in the CUDA source; the Triton fallback simply lacks the corresponding term. The asymmetry looks like an unmirrored branch, not a semantic choice. 3. **Parity is the actual contract.** Two implementations of one op differing is the bug; which semantics wins is secondary. Choosing the main path's makes the fix a pure consistency correction with a tiny review surface. A PR implementing the above follows this issue. If maintainers prefer the fallback's finer floor for tiny values, the same patch flips trivially — but we'd treat that as a separate primary-kernel behavior change, not part of this parity fix. --- *Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the reporter; the diagnosis and reported hardware observations were verified by the reporter.*
