signals.title: [Bugfix][Optimization] Zero packed KV blocks once from the backing sorage base
signals.text: ## Problem `KVBlockZeroer` builds one segment per aliased layer view of a packed block-first KV cache (e.g. DeepSeek V4). Each segment starts at the layer view's `data_ptr()`. Packed views are created by `_reshape_attention_kv_cache`: kv_cache = kv_raw_tensor.view(-1, block_stride)[:, offset : offset + page_bytes] For such a view: - `kv.data_ptr()` includes the layer's per-block byte `offset` - `kv.stride(block_dim) * element_size()` is the whole slab's per-block stride, not this layer's page size Starting a segment at `data_ptr()` therefore zeroes: backing_base + layer_offset + block_id * block_stride which has two failure modes: 1. **Out-of-bounds write** — for `layer_offset > 0`, the last blocks walk past the end of the backing allocation (CUDA illegal memory access), reproduced as `block_id = num_blocks - 1` failing while `num_blocks - 2` is safe. 2. **Cross-layer stomp** — even in bounds, the cleared range is shifted by `layer_offset`, overwriting a neighbouring layer's KV (session corruption). ## Fix Root every segment at the backing storage base and deduplicate on the storage pointer so each packed slab is zeroed exactly once, and make the cleared span cover the whole block stride: 1. `dp = kv.untyped_storage().data_ptr()` — strips the per-block layer offset. 2. deduplicate on `dp` (storage base) — one segment per packed slab. 3. `seg_page_sizes` uses `block_stride_bytes` instead of the single-layer `kernel_page_bytes` — a single segment clears every interleaved layer. All three changes are required together: starting at the storage base without widening the span would clear only the first layer, and widening the span without rooting at the storage base would shift the cleared region. ## Correctness | layout | storage base | span | dedup | result | |---|---|---|---|---| | packed block-first | != data_ptr | whole block | 1 seg / slab | clears all layers, no OOB | | standalone allocation | == data_ptr | == page size | 1 seg / layer | unchanged | | K/V-first (block_dim=1) | == data_ptr | == page size | K/V segments | unchanged | | page-aligned (ROCm) | == data_ptr | == page size | unchanged | unchanged | The key invariant is that `kv.stride(block_dim) * element_size()` always equals the full byte span of one logical block: the sum of all layer pages for packed views, and the single-layer page size for standalone allocations. Setting `seg_page_sizes == seg_block_strides == block_stride_bytes // 4` therefore clears exactly one whole block per segment. ## Performance The kernel grid becomes `(n_blocks, n_segs, max_chunks)` where `max_chunks` grows from `single_layer_page / blk_size` to `block_stride / blk_size`. Total kernel programs are unchanged (`N_layers x small` -> `1 x large`), but the number of kernel launches per zeroing step drops from `N_layers` to 1. ## Test - `test_packed_slab_dedup_clears_whole_block` — two layers sharing a packed backing yield a single segment rooted at the storage base with `block_stride` as the cleared span; zeroing the last block clears the whole block. - `test_packed_segment_zeros_whole_block_from_storage_base` (replaces `test_packed_segment_zeros_only_its_last_block_page`) — verifies a packed segment rooted at the storage base clears the full block stride, not a single layer's page. ## Relationship to #50276 #50276 (already merged) splits block stride from page span but keeps per-layer segments starting at `data_ptr()`. This PR is a complementary alternative: it collapses the per-layer segments of a packed slab into one whole-block segment rooted at the storage base. This both removes the offset-based OOB/stomp hazard and reduces zeroing launches from `N_layers` to 1. The two approaches are mutually exclusive for packed views; this PR does not layer on top of #50276 but replaces the per-layer segment construction for the packed case.

signals.title: feat(rust): accept preprocessed multimodal gRPC features
signals.text: ## Summary Add an independent Rust gRPC adapter for preprocessed multimodal feature specs. ## Why Callers that already produce version-compatible engine-ready multimodal kwargs should be able to pass those features directly, avoiding duplicate media preprocessing in the Rust frontend and mapping to Python `MultiModalFeatureSpec`. ## Changes - Add a protobuf source variant for inline preprocessed features. - Decode MessagePack `MmKwargsItem` data and lower it to EngineCore features. - Keep existing raw-image handling unchanged. - Require inline kwargs; cache-only references are intentionally unsupported. - Derive the EngineCore cache identity from modality and payload bytes. - Validate payload size, MessagePack complexity, tensor metadata, field metadata, placeholder ranges, and auxiliary-frame references at the gRPC boundary. ## Scope This is an independent gRPC adapter and does not depend on the routed-experts changes. It is a supported subset of the Python frontend contract, not a claim of full Python API parity. ## Checks - `cargo fmt --all -- --check` - `cargo test -p vllm-server grpc` (54 passed) ## Review note This change was prepared with AI assistance and reviewed line by line before submission.

signals.title: feat(rust): expose routed expert traces over gRPC
signals.text: ## Summary Expose routed-expert capture through the Rust gRPC request and terminal response path. ## Why The Rust frontend needs a northbound API that can request routed-expert capture and return the decoded native EngineCore trace to non-Python clients without adopting a client-specific response envelope. ## Changes - use the merged `routed_experts_prompt_start` request control in gRPC response options - validate and lower the request-side prompt offset - accumulate routed-expert chunks while enforcing a stable dtype and trailing shape - return a typed terminal tensor containing only bytes, shape, and dtype - keep the prompt start out of the tensor because it is request context, not native routed-output data - keep OpenAI route behavior unchanged; constructor updates only initialize the new internal field - add gRPC round-trip, aggregation, and invalid-offset coverage Python vLLM's public format remains Base64 `.npy`. The typed tensor is an internal gRPC representation; downstream public compatibility layers serialize it to native `.npy` rather than a framework-specific object. ## Stack dependencies 1. #52721 supplies typed EngineCore routed-output decoding and native NumPy serialization. 2. #52703 supplied the Python-compatible sampling field and is already merged. This branch contains #52721 so the end-to-end path can be reviewed and tested. After #52721 merges, the final diff contains only terminal aggregation and the gRPC surface. It is independent of #52722. ## Checks - `cargo fmt --all -- --check` - focused gRPC conversion and round-trip tests passed on the rebuilt branch - DCO-restacked review head `76fe721765561483a366747344df2a6c5cd1d56d` has the same Git tree as the GPU-tested head - integrated small Qwen3-MoE validation completed pre-training capture, three training steps, policy version 1 transfer, and post-update routed capture ## Review note This change was prepared with AI assistance and reviewed line by line before submission.

signals.title: [Attention] Enable adaptive verification for FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4
signals.text: ## Purpose Follow-up to #47808. The FlashInfer sparse MLA decode kernel (`flashinfer_trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4`) supports variable query lengths via `cum_seq_lens_q` / `max_q_len`, but the backend's metadata builders reported `AttentionCGSupport.UNIFORM_BATCH` instead of `ALWAYS`. Adds thin metadata builder subclasses (MLA + SWA) that declare `AttentionCGSupport.ALWAYS`, mirroring the pattern established by the FlashMLA backend in `flashmla.py`, and wires them into `DeepseekV4FlashInferMLASparseBackend` and both attention classes. ## Test Plan - Existing `tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py` validates FlashInfer sparse MLA kernel correctness (no behavioural change to the forward path). - End-to-end: run DeepSeek-V4 with `enable_adaptive_verification: true` on FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV4 — the runtime assertion that previously raised the error now passes. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signals.title: [MooncakeStore] Report KV load tier in cache events
signals.text: ## Purpose Report the actual MooncakeStore replica tier in KV cache events. Mooncake already exposes whether a loaded replica is memory-backed or disk-backed, but this information was not propagated to `BlockStored` events. This change maps: * memory-backed replica → `CPU` * disk-backed replica → `STORAGE` * unknown tier → `None` Successful events are emitted only for blocks that actually load successfully. Scheduler lookup and connector protocol behavior are unchanged. ## Test Plan Run the focused MooncakeStore worker tests: ```bash python -m pytest \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_worker.py \ -v \ --confcutdir=tests/v1/kv_connector/unit \ -k "test_recv_thread_emits_tiered_events_after_rotation_and_split or test_recv_thread_emits_unknown_tier_with_no_medium or test_recv_thread_does_not_emit_event_for_failed_load or test_recv_thread_skips_tier_lookup_when_events_and_logging_disabled" ``` Also run an end-to-end MooncakeStore smoke test on the DGX/A100 setup to exercise the real replica-tier lookup path. ## Test Results ### Focused unit tests ```text 4 passed, 112 deselected in 7.02s ``` Validated: * memory-backed replicas map to `CPU` * disk-backed replicas map to `STORAGE` * unknown tier leaves `medium` unset * failed loads do not emit successful `BlockStored` events * replica-tier lookup is skipped when both KV events and tier logging are disabled * block hashes remain correctly aligned through rotation and disk-budget splitting ### Integration smoke test Ran vLLM with MooncakeStore on an A100 using a 256 MB embedded Mooncake segment. A real Mooncake-backed reload reported: ```text batch_keys=35 memory_keys=35 disk_keys=0 unknown_keys=0 success_keys=35 failed_keys=0 bytes_by_tier={'memory': 82575360, 'disk': 0, 'unknown': 0} ``` This confirms that the runtime replica metadata path correctly identifies real memory-backed loads. Disk persistence was also exercised successfully, but a disk-only reload could not be observed with the embedded-store setup because the in-memory replica remains available. A true disk-backed reload would require a standalone-store configuration. The focused unit tests directly validate the disk-replica → `STORAGE` event mapping.

signals.title: fix(build): correct preprocessor guard for GDN decode to fix Ampere c…
signals.text: fused_gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp was mistakenly placed inside the VLLM_ENABLE_FUSED_KDA_DECODE block in ops.h. Since KDA is restricted to SM90+, this caused compilation to fail on pre-Hopper architectures (like Ampere SM 8.6) which support GDN but not KDA. This commit moves the declaration to the correct VLLM_ENABLE_FUSED_GDN_DECODE guard. ## Purpose Building vLLM from source fails on Ampere (SM 8.6) and other pre-Hopper architectures with the following error: `error: ‘fused_gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp’ was not declared in this scope` This occurs because `fused_gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp` in `csrc/libtorch_stable/ops.h` was mistakenly placed inside the `#ifdef VLLM_ENABLE_FUSED_KDA_DECODE` preprocessor block. Because KDA requires SM90+ (Hopper) or newer, the `VLLM_ENABLE_FUSED_KDA_DECODE` flag is not defined on Ampere systems. However, GDN is supported on Ampere (`VLLM_ENABLE_FUSED_GDN_DECODE=1`), so `torch_bindings.cpp` attempts to bind the GDN function, resulting in a compilation failure since the declaration is missing. ## Solution Separated the declarations. Moved `fused_gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp` out of the KDA block and placed it under its correct `#ifdef VLLM_ENABLE_FUSED_GDN_DECODE` preprocessor guard. ## Test - Verified that `pip install -e .` successfully compiles and installs on an Ampere (SM 8.6) system without build errors. --- <summary> Simple fix to ensure the fused_gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp compiles under all archs and not just post ampere archs by placing the function under VLLM_ENABLE_FUSED_GDN_DECODE preprocessor guard</summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details> **BEFORE SUBMITTING, PLEASE READ <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing>** (anything written below this line will be removed by GitHub Actions) co author: Gemini

signals.text: ## Summary This PR optimizes #51324 with the following improvements: - Resolve shared/private Host pool mode in the KV cache planner. - Fall back to private pools when the Indexer block layout cannot be represented by the shared mmap layout. - Propagate the resolved mode and physical Host block stride through `KVCacheConfig`. - Roll back the shared Host region when GPU KV allocation or HiSparse worker initialization fails. - Check physical Host RAM only in the shared mmap creator process. - Fail joiners promptly when the creator fails and unlinks an incomplete mmap. - Add real multiprocess same-slot visibility coverage. - Clarify logical versus physical `host_pool_gib` capacity and startup logging. signals.title: [Bugfix][KV Connector][NIXL] Support PCP producers
signals.text: ## Purpose Support NIXL P/D disaggregation when the producer uses prefill context parallelism (PCP) and decode context parallelism (DCP) is disabled on both sides. PCP expands the worker world without increasing the KV-cache shard count, so every PCP rank holds an equivalent KV replica. NIXL should publish and wait for one replica instead of treating all PCP workers as distinct KV shards. This change: - records each NIXL worker's PCP rank; - publishes handshake metadata only from PCP rank zero on a producer; - forwards producer send completions only from PCP rank zero; - aggregates PCP producer completions over `TP * PP`; and - rejects PCP consumers, `kv_both`, and combined PCP+DCP configurations. It does not change the NIXL handshake protocol, worker addressing, transfer topology, KV layout, or token mapping. ## Scope and related work This PR is intentionally limited to `DCP=1` on both producer and consumer. It does not enable consumer-side PCP or combined PCP+DCP layouts. PR #50611 owns NIXL DCP support and its shard-routing/configuration changes. This PR is complementary: it only selects a canonical replica along the PCP axis when no DCP sharding exists. The duplicate-work searches for `NIXL PCP`, `prefill context parallel NIXL`, and `PCP producer KV connector` found #38433, #45340, #49109, #49342, and #50611. None implements this PCP-only NIXL replica selection on current main: - #50611 handles DCP sharding and currently requires PCP to be disabled. - #45340 handles CP-scaled scheduler block accounting. - #49109 is Mooncake-specific. - #49342 is the older mixed PCP+DCP version of this work and is superseded by this smaller PR. ## Tests ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_output_aggregator.py \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_connector.py \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_nixl_push_connector.py \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_multi_connector.py \ -k "not abort_timeout_on_prefiller and not register_kv_caches and not reqs_to_send_deadline_rebased_to_worker_clock" \ -q # 144 passed, 7 deselected ``` ```bash .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files <changed files> # passed ``` Four-GPU P/D validation on `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat`: - Producer: `TP=1, PCP=2, DCP=1, EP=2` - Consumer: `TP=2, PCP=1, DCP=1, EP=2` - NIXL transport: local UCX TCP/CUDA IPC - Final-commit smoke: four prompts passed, including a long multi-block transfer - GSM8K: 1,319 questions, 5-shot, accuracy `0.636846`, invalid rate `0.000758` (159,800 output tokens) ```bash chg run -g 4 --timeout 45m -- env \ MODEL=deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat \ GSM8K_QUESTIONS=1319 GSM8K_CONCURRENCY=64 \ bash ./pd_test.sh pcp2-nodcp-gsm8k \ '--tensor-parallel-size 1 --prefill-context-parallel-size 2 --enable-expert-parallel --max-num-batched-tokens 2048' \ '--tensor-parallel-size 2 --enable-expert-parallel' ``` ## AI assistance disclosure OpenAI Codex assisted with investigation, implementation, testing, and drafting this PR. The human submitter remains responsible for reviewing every changed line and understanding and defending the change end-to-end.

signals.title: [Spec Decode] Enable adaptive DSpark on SM100 sparse MLA
signals.text: ## Purpose Resolves #52785. This is part of the adaptive DSpark backend expansion tracked by #51303. Related GLM-5.2 DSpark bring-up context is in #50851. This enables adaptive DSpark verification with `FlashInferMLASparseTRTLLMBackend`. It was validated end to end with `nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4` and `RedHatAI/GLM-5.2-speculator.dspark` on 4× NVIDIA B300. Before this change, startup failed for two independent reasons: 1. The sparse-MLA metadata builder derived token-to-request mappings from CPU query boundaries. Adaptive verification changes those boundaries on device without synchronizing them back to the CPU. 2. The target graph capability check included the draft model's FlashAttention backend. Draft attention is captured and capability-checked by its own graph manager, and it never consumes the target's adaptive query lengths. ## Changes - Add an SM100 FlashInfer sparse-MLA metadata builder that derives request IDs from device query boundaries and declares variable-length CUDA graph support. - Scope target CUDA graph and query-length compatibility checks to target attention layers while retaining draft groups needed by draft prefill. - Add a real B300 kernel regression using GLM-5.2 dimensions. It compares FlashInfer sparse MLA against SDPA with device query lengths `[1, 7, 3, 5]` and deliberately stale CPU lengths `[4, 4, 4, 4]`. - Add a unit regression proving draft-only groups are excluded without hiding mixed target/draft groups that still participate in target execution. ## Performance Scaled SPEED Bench qualitative sweep, 16K context, 512 output tokens, temperature 1.0, seed 0. The c1 run used 32 prompts, c16 used 128, and the remaining points used 256. Both configurations completed with zero failed requests. | Concurrency | Fixed k=7 tok/s | Adaptive tok/s | Gain | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 306.7 | 310.6 | +1.3% | | 16 | 2,084.4 | 2,093.5 | +0.4% | | 32 | 3,525.0 | 3,595.8 | +2.0% | | 64 | 5,236.8 | 5,538.8 | +5.8% | | 128 | 7,172.9 | 8,190.7 | +14.2% | | 256 | 7,720.4 | 10,316.8 | +33.6% | At c256, mean TPOT improved from 23.24 ms to 17.37 ms. A direct B300 kernel comparison also favored the selected FlashInfer SM100 backend over FlashMLA by 2.1–2.6× for uniform decode batches and 31.9× for a mixed 1/3/5/7-token adaptive shape. ## Model evaluation GSM8K, five-shot, 200 examples, greedy decoding, 2,048-token output limit: | Configuration | Accuracy | Invalid/truncated | |---|---:|---:| | Fixed k=7 | 89.0% | 1.0% | | Adaptive k≤7 | 91.0% | 0.5% | This shows no detected accuracy regression at this sample size; the two-point difference is not presented as statistically significant. HLE was also exercised, but 38/40 sampled outputs still truncated at an 8,192-token limit, so no HLE accuracy result is reported. ## Reproduction ```bash chg run -g=4 -- vllm serve nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --load-format instanttensor \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --block-size 64 \ --max-model-len 16384 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \ --max-num-seqs 256 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8 \ --compilation-config '{"max_cudagraph_capture_size":2048}' \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"RedHatAI/GLM-5.2-speculator.dspark","attention_backend":"FLASH_ATTN","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","enable_adaptive_verification":true}' ``` The full server completed target and draft CUDA graph capture and served the benchmark/evaluation requests successfully. ## Test plan ```bash chg run -g=1 -- .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/v1/attention/test_dspark_noncausal_sparse_mla.py -q # 21 passed, 8 skipped .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py -q # 7 passed .venv/bin/pre-commit run ruff-check --files .venv/bin/pre-commit run ruff-format --files .venv/bin/pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files # all passed ``` The focused CPU and B300 tests plus lint and mypy were rerun after rebasing onto current `main`. ## Not a duplicate Duplicate checks covered #51303 and adaptive DSpark/sparse-MLA keywords. #52362 enables adaptive verification on ROCm and changes AMD model/indexer paths; it does not overlap this CUDA SM100 metadata and target/draft graph-scoping change. #50694 addresses earlier FA3 and DSpark/DFlash proposer wiring for GLM-5.2. ## AI assistance AI assistance (OpenAI Codex) was used to investigate, implement, test, benchmark, and draft this change. The submitter reviewed every changed line, understands the change end to end, and ran the tests and model evaluations reported above.

signals.title: [Perf] Support internal prefill checkpoints for Mamba prefix caching, 9%~25% TTFT improvement
signals.text: ## Purpose Mamba prefix caching currently splits a prefill at the last block boundary Let's use a 8k input as an example Before ```bash Model forward (7680 tokens) -> FlashKDA(7680 tokens) -> save checkpoint -> Model forward (320 tokens) -> FlashKDA(320 tokens) ``` Now ```bash Model forward (8000 tokens) -> FlashKDA(7680) -> save checkpoint -> FlashKDA(320) ``` This PR helps us avoid a second full-model pass through attention, MoE, routing, and TP collectives. ## Test ```bash vllm serve moonshotai/Kimi-K3 \ --trust-remote-code \ -tp 8 \ --load-format fastsafetensors \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --reasoning-parser kimi_k3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser kimi_k3 \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 30000 ``` Acc covered in unit tests Perf ```bash HF_HUB_CACHE=/data/engine/hub_cache HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 guidellm run --backend '{"kind":"openai_http","target":"http://127.0.0.1:30000","model":"moonshotai/Kimi-K3","request_format":"/v1/chat/completions","timeout":100000,"extras":{"body":{"reasoning_effort":"max","temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95}}}' --tokenizer '{"kind":"huggingface_auto","model":"moonshotai/Kimi-K3","load_kwargs":{"trust_remote_code":true,"local_files_only":true}}' --data 'kind=synthetic_text,prompt_tokens=8000,output_tokens=1000' --profile 'kind=concurrent,warmup=0.1,cooldown=0.1' --override profile.streams '1,4,16' --constraint 'kind=max_duration,seconds=150' --constraint 'kind=max_errors,count=10' --seed 'kind=static,value=42' --metrics 'kind=generative,sample_size=20' --output 'kind=json,path=/home/yewentao256/guidellm-results/output_vllm_kimik3_8k1k.json' ``` And we get Huge TTFT improvement Concurrency | Before | After | Improvement -- | -- | -- | -- 1 | 435.28 ms | 394.19 ms | 9.4%🚀 4 | 1450.94 ms | 1080.78 ms | 25.5%🚀 16 | 2648.48 ms | 2099.69 ms | 20.7%🚀 Other metrics Concurrency | Prompt tokens/s ↑ | Request latency ↓ -- | -- | -- 1 | 789.55 -> 821.00 (+4.0%) | 10.243 -> 9.851 s (-3.8%) 4 | 1202.37 -> 1219.29 (+1.4%) | 14.447 -> 13.951 s (-3.4%) 16 | 848.57 -> 868.86 (+2.4%) | 23.986 -> 23.937 s (-0.2%) </body></html> [output_sglang_kimik3_8k1k.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31186873/output_sglang_kimik3_8k1k.json) [output_vllm_kimik3_8k1k_no_spec.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31186874/output_vllm_kimik3_8k1k_no_spec.json) Following up tasks: - Spec decoding support - More tasks support - Update flashKDA so we can avoid twice kernel call

signals.title: [Bugfix][Attention] Normalize FlashInfer prefill LSE before merging
signals.text: ## Purpose Prefix-cache hits could produce different logits from a cold prefill and eventually lead to repetitive output. This was initially observed with GLM-5.2 in a disaggregated prefill/decode deployment. KV cache digests matched before and after transfer, and the issue also reproduced with BF16 KV cache. A local prefix-cache cold/warm comparison then reproduced the logits divergence without KV transfer, narrowing the issue to the cached-context attention path. A cold prefill computes attention in one operation. On a prefix-cache hit, vLLM computes attention over the cached context and new suffix separately, then combines the two partial states with `merge_attn_states`. FlashInfer prefill kernels, including the TRT-LLM ragged kernel, return base-2 log-sum-exp values. vLLM's CUDA and Triton `merge_attn_states` implementations use natural `exp` and `log`. Passing base-2 LSE values directly therefore produces incorrect context/suffix weights. This PR: - adds a shared `log2_lse_to_ln` conversion helper; - converts LSE returned by the FlashInfer MLA prefill backend; - converts LSE returned by the TRT-LLM ragged MLA prefill backend; - converts generic FlashInfer DCP prefill LSE after the base-2 cross-rank reduction and before the natural-log attention-state merge. The conversion is performed at the external kernel boundary so the rest of vLLM continues to use the natural-log LSE contract. ### Duplicate-work check No open PR currently fixes the MLA prefill paths changed here. PR #36503 previously experimented with scaling generic FlashInfer prefill LSE in an older commit (`f10579e`), but that change is not present in its current diff. Its current scope is persistent buffer management for FlashInfer DCP decode. This PR fixes the missing conversions on current main and additionally covers both FlashInfer MLA prefill and TRT-LLM ragged MLA prefill. PR #47779 concerns SM120 sparse MLA decode DCP and does not modify these prefill merge paths. ## Test Plan ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -rs \ tests/v1/attention/test_mla_backends.py \ -k 'test_chunked_context_backend_correctness and \ (FLASHINFER or TRTLLM_RAGGED)' .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \ vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py \ vllm/v1/attention/backends/flashinfer.py \ vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/prefill/flashinfer.py \ vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/prefill/trtllm_ragged.py git diff --check ``` Before/after error measurements used the same B300 GPU, test selection, and random sequence. The old behavior was simulated by replacing the conversion helper with an identity function at runtime. ## Test Result Affected auto/FP8 matrix: - 6 passed - 2 skipped because FlashInfer does not support the tested GLM dimensions Maximum absolute output error against the SDPA reference: | Prefill path | Before | After | | --- | ---: | ---: | | FlashInfer / DeepSeek | 0.236328 | 0.0078125 | | TRT-LLM ragged / DeepSeek | 0.228516 | 0.0078125 | | TRT-LLM ragged / GLM | 0.265625 | 0.0078125 | The results were identical across CUTLASS_MLA, FLASHINFER_MLA, and TRITON_MLA, which is consistent with the error originating in the shared context/suffix merge. Pre-commit and `git diff --check` passed. The complete `test_chunked_context_backend_correctness` matrix produced 10 passed, 8 skipped, and 2 failures. Both failures are in the unchanged FlashAttention FA4 path because the local extension does not accept the `fp8_kv_dequant` keyword. signals.title: [Bugfix][KV Offload] Do not let a recurrent group's unhashed block truncate the load boundary
signals.text: `update_state_after_alloc` scans the allocated block list for the first block that is `not is_null and block_hash is None` and treats that index as the start of the freshly allocated region. That index is load-bearing: it drives [`start_chunk_idx` / `keys_to_load`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py), `dst_block_ids`, `group_sizes` and `block_indices`. Getting it wrong loads the wrong keys into the wrong destination blocks. The scan started at **index 0** — inside the region already reported as locally computed, where every block is computed by definition. For a **recurrent (Mamba / GDN) group** that is not merely redundant but wrong. Such a group has no per-token KV at all: it carries a fixed-size state, which is why `get_sliding_window_size_in_chunks()` returns 1 for `MambaSpec` ("Mamba depends on a single state"). Most positions in its block table point at the shared null sentinel, and the one real block holding the state is legitimately **not full-and-cached** — non-null, unhashed, sitting below the computed mark. ``` legend [H] hashed [·] null placeholder [U] non-null, UNHASHED [F] fresh recurrent group (GDN/Mamba, window = 1 chunk), 21 chunks computed + 1 loaded: idx 0 1 2 3 4 ... 20 21 [H] [H] [·] [U] [·] ... [·] [F] ^ BEFORE scan starts at 0, stops here boundary = 3 |<-------- claimed computed: 21 ------------>| assert 21 <= 3 ✗ AssertionError load region would be blocks 3..21 -> 19 wrong destinations, wrong keys AFTER scan starts at first_fresh = 21 ------------>^ boundary = 21, assert 21 <= 21 ✓ load region = block 21 only -> matches the 1-chunk hit ``` For a full-attention group this is a **no-op**: every token has KV, every block below the boundary is full-and-cached, so the old scan skipped them anyway. The existing assert now holds by construction (`nlcgb >= cdiv(nlct, tpb)` ⟹ `nlct <= nlcgb * tpb`); it is kept as a guard against other causes rather than deleted. ## Reproduction 4-node GB200, Qwen3.5-family hybrid GDN+GQA (4 KV cache groups, 3 recurrent), MTP, 384 GiB host tier. Under sustained load the leader crashed after **47,142 requests**: ``` File "vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 963, in schedule self.connector.update_state_after_alloc( File ".../kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py", line 832, in update_state_after_alloc num_locally_computed_tokens AssertionError leader exit=1 | other three exit=137 (gang teardown) ``` The captured 3h22m window on the crashing rank makes the trigger unambiguous. It saw **22 lookups that hit offloaded tokens, but only 4 that were true partial hits** (`num_locally_computed_tokens > 0`) — and all four arrived in the last 36 seconds: | time | external tokens | locally computed | outcome | |---|---|---|---| | 00:57 – 04:18 | 18 lookups | **0** | fine — assert reads `0 <= X` | | 04:18:45 | 4256 | 8512 | ok | | 04:18:52 | 2128 | 4256 | ok | | 04:19:07 | 2128 | 10640 | ok | | 04:19:21 | 4256 | 10640 | **AssertionError, same second** | **Why this is easy to miss.** It needs `num_external_tokens > 0` **and** `num_locally_computed_tokens > 0`. Tests that flood to full eviction before re-sending produce `num_computed_tokens == 0` — 18 of the 22 lookups above — where the assert reads `0 <= X` and cannot fire. The rank sat clean for 3h21m under exactly that pattern before the first partial hits appeared. ### Reproduced on a build that carries the #49146 clamp The assert is **not** masked by [#49146](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49146)'s `num_allocated_chunks` clamp (`94ed0bf4e0`, in `main`). A build composed as `#49146 clamp + #52771, without this fix` was put under sustained production traffic and asserted **three times across two independent clusters**, at roughly **20 minutes / ~850 requests** each: ``` vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:963 schedule vllm/.../kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py:840 update_state_after_alloc AssertionError ``` Line 840 is this assert: in the same tree without the clamp it sits at 832, and the clamp inserts exactly 8 lines above it — the two tracebacks are the same assertion. Across four builds under the same workload and config, the correlation is with **this fix**, not the clamp and not #52771: | build | #49146 clamp | #52771 | this fix | fault-free lifetime | |---|---|---|---|---| | A | — | — | — | 22–70 min, 3 asserts | | B | — | ✓ | — | 10 / 30 / 40 / 88 min, ≥4 asserts | | C | ✓ | ✓ | — | ~20 min, 3 asserts | | D | ✓ | — | ✓ | **336 min, zero asserts** | Every build lacking this fix asserts, including one carrying the clamp; the only build carrying it is the only one that holds. Memory was never implicated (no `OOMKilled`; peak well under limit). A separate note on reproducing it: a synthetic driver that holds the hit *shape* constant does not surface this. On a smaller same-family deployment I drove **12,000 consecutive requests at a 100% true-partial-hit rate** with no assert — but every request had an identical `num_locally_computed_tokens`, so it probed one boundary alignment repeatedly. The production crashes arise under organically varied prefix lengths, which is what walks the boundary across block offsets. ## Relationship to #52735 / #52771 **This is independent of the drafter-annotation defect, and of the abort fix.** Three arms, all at current `main` (which already carries the [#49146](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49146) `num_allocated_chunks` clamp, commit `94ed0bf4e0`), running the regression test below: | arm | #49146 clamp | #52771 | this fix | `offloading_connector/` suite | |---|---|---|---|---| | A | ✓ (in `main`) | — | — | regression test **fails** | | B | ✓ | ✓ | — | **1 failed**, 254 passed | | C | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | **255 passed, 0 failed** | Arms B and C were run back-to-back in a single GPU allocation, toggling only this hunk, so the environment is identical; the one failure in B is this PR's regression test and nothing else. Every test that passes without the fix still passes with it. Arm B is the decisive one: with #52771 (`44a3045ec1`) cherry-picked on top of `main`, the all-groups drafter fallback removed and no group marked as a drafter — so the volatile-tail pop never runs — the boundary assert still fires. The assert is not gated on `is_eagle_group` anywhere. #52771 is also **complementary**: by restoring real loads it raises how often `num_external_tokens > 0`, and therefore how often this path is reached. It is the right fix for the annotation defect and should land; this is the crash underneath it. *(This PR previously also carried a competing fix for #52735 — removing the eagle query-widen, `required_window += 1` and the volatile-tail pop. I have dropped all of it in favour of #52771, which was filed first, targets the root cause rather than the symptom, and additionally fixes a store-side hole mine did not. What remains here is only the boundary fix.)* ## Tests `test_recurrent_group_unhashed_block_does_not_truncate_load_boundary` plants exactly that block — non-null, unhashed, below the boundary — and asserts the **destination blocks** are correct (`41 not in loaded`, `42 in loaded`), not merely that nothing raised. Verified to **fail against unpatched `main`** and pass with this change. Full `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/` suite green on an aarch64 GB200 node.

signals.title: [Spec Decode] DFlash2: local convolution + candidate selector
signals.text: Two additions to the DFlash drafter, carried by a separate architecture: a checkpoint declaring `DFlash2DraftModel` gets them, and every existing `DFlashDraftModel` checkpoint resolves to the class it resolves to today, untouched by this PR. **Grouped dynamic depthwise convolution** inside each block, so a proposal position can see the ones before it without another backbone pass. `out[i,c] = Σ_t (base[t,c] + δ[i,t,g(c)]) · x[i−t,c]`, taps zero across the block boundary. Wraps each sublayer in and out from one projection of its input. Sized by `conv_kernel_size` and `conv_group_size` in the draft config. **Candidate selector.** Instead of an independent argmax per slot, keep the target head's top-K per slot, score adjacent transitions `edge(p→c) = ⟨A[p] ⊙ project(h), B[c]⟩ + unary[c]`, and walk the best path from the verified anchor. At T>0 it walks by inverse CDF and returns q over the K candidates for the lossless verify. Sized by `selector_rank` and `selector_top_k` in the draft config. ``` model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py the convolution and the selector v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dflash2/speculator.py the walk kernel and the proposal model_executor/models/registry.py DFlash2DraftModel v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/__init__.py speculator selection ``` The selector runs after the draft model's forward and carries its own `@support_torch_compile`. The path walk is one Triton program per request: a slot's K scores stay in registers, and the slot-to-slot dependency is a loop inside the program rather than a kernel per slot. The vocabulary top-k, the selector's largest single cost, uses FlashInfer's radix kernel where FlashInfer is available and `torch.topk` otherwise. DFlash2 runs on the V2 model runner, which is where its speculator lives. `use_v2_model_runner` selects V2 for a DFlash2 draft, as it already does for DSpark: the V1 `DFlashProposer` has no candidate selector, so a DFlash2 checkpoint reaching it would draft as DFlash1 without raising. ## Results `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` on one H200, against [`RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark`](https://huggingface.co/RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark) and autoregressive decoding. Seven draft tokens per verification step for both drafters. Qwen3.8's recommended sampling — temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20 — with `xhigh` reasoning effort and 4096 max new tokens; prompt formatting from [`z-lab/dflash`](https://github.com/z-lab/dflash). ### Acceptance length, GSM8K Mean over per-request acceptance, the statistic the model cards report. vLLM's counters give a pooled ratio — total accepted tokens over total drafts — so the per-request values are recovered at concurrency 1, where a counter delta around a single request belongs to that request alone. | | DSpark | DFlash 2 | | |---|-------:|---------:|---| | per-request mean | 4.27 | **5.34** | +25.2% | | pooled ratio | 3.64 | **4.65** | +27.8% | Acceptance does not move with concurrency: DFlash 2's pooled ratio reads 4.65, 4.82 and 4.74 at concurrency 1, 8 and 32. ### Throughput, GSM8K Output tokens over end-to-end wall time. Each point is 128 × concurrency requests split over four shards, each shard one H200 serving at the stated concurrency; the four shard rates are averaged, not summed, so a cell is a single-GPU number measured four times. A warmup of `concurrency` requests runs before the clock starts and is dropped, as in `z-lab/dflash`. | conc | requests | autoregressive | DSpark | DFlash 2 | |------|---------:|---------------:|-------:|---------:| | 1 | 124 | 64.1 | 178.5 (2.79×) | **224.6 (3.51×)** | | 8 | 992 | 416.4 | 966.2 (2.32×) | **1,211.7 (2.91×)** | | 32 | 3,968 | 1,256.9 | 2,220.9 (1.77×) | **2,759.4 (2.20×)** | All three methods are served one after another inside the same container, so a difference between them is never a difference between GPUs. Spread across the four shards is 2.1–2.5% for autoregressive and 2.6–15.2% for the drafters, which is the shape to expect: a drafter's rate depends on which prompts it drew and autoregressive decoding has no such freedom. ### What the conv and the selector cost Each component timed alone in its own CUDA graph at the shapes the draft runs (5 layers, hidden 5120, vocab 248320, block 8, K=16), against the measured serving step — draft proposal plus target verification — taken from the run above as `pooled acceptance × concurrency / tok s`. | batch | conv | top-k | lattice | walk | selector | conv+selector | step | share | |-------|-----:|------:|--------:|-----:|---------:|--------------:|-----:|------:| | 1 | 0.113 | 0.041 | 0.014 | 0.006 | 0.061 | **0.174 ms** | 20.70 ms | **0.84%** | | 8 | 0.121 | 0.084 | 0.016 | 0.006 | 0.106 | **0.227 ms** | 31.80 ms | **0.71%** | | 32 | 0.173 | 0.173 | 0.018 | 0.006 | 0.197 | **0.370 ms** | 54.93 ms | **0.67%** | The selector's own math — the lattice and the walk — is 0.020 ms and flat in batch; the rest of that column is the vocabulary top-k, where FlashInfer's radix kernel is 1.9× `torch.topk` at batch 1 and 4.5× at batch 32. The convolution is 20 small calls over `[8, 5120]` tensors, so it is launch-bound rather than FLOP-bound: 0.477 ms as eager modules, 0.0096 ms compiled as a single graph across all 20 calls, and 0.113 ms — the figure above — with each call compiled on its own, which is what the model's compiled region gives it, since attention and the MLP run between `prepare` and `finish`. A hand-fused kernel would collect most of the remaining 12×. ## Test Result ``` pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash2.py 4 passed pytest tests/test_config.py::test_dflash2_draft_forces_v2... 1 passed pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_causality.py \ tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_lookahead.py \ tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py 19 passed ``` The three DFlash v1 files pass unchanged. `test_dflash_causality.py` is edited here, in the same change that touches `_dflash_layer_causal`, so its updated tests do not by themselves speak to v1 compatibility; the versions of those tests as they stood before this change also pass against this tree. Serving results are the tables above: GSM8K at three concurrencies on `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B`, run through vLLM's OpenAI server, 128 × concurrency requests per point. ## Not a duplicate `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "DFlash in:title"` returns work on the existing DFlash v1 path — adaptive K (#52559), SWA (#47511), fused cache insert (#46911), profiling annotations (#52782) — and `--search "dflash2"` returns nothing. This adds the DFlash2 drafter, which none of those touch. AI assistance was used for this change.

signals.title: [DSv4 Perf] Adaptive topk width for dsv4, making #50004 back
signals.text: ## Purpose https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50004 was reverted by https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51318 This PR get the similar performance gain but doesn't hurt the accuracy ## Test ### Perf E2E perf see https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50004 Kernel level perf can be seen in this AI generated script ```bash # SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 # SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright contributors to the vLLM project """Benchmark adaptive-width DeepSeek-V4 C128A prefill metadata.""" import torch from vllm.models.deepseek_v4.sparse_mla import build_c128a_topk_metadata from vllm.triton_utils import triton NUM_TOKENS = [512, 2048, 8192, 32768] CONTEXT_LEN = 32768 COMPRESS_RATIO = 128 CAPACITY_WIDTH = 8192 ACTIVE_WIDTH = max(triton.next_power_of_2(CONTEXT_LEN // COMPRESS_RATIO), 128) def benchmark(num_tokens: int, width: int) -> float: device = torch.device("cuda") positions = torch.arange( CONTEXT_LEN - num_tokens, CONTEXT_LEN, dtype=torch.int64, device=device, ) global_decode_buffer = torch.empty( (1, CAPACITY_WIDTH), dtype=torch.int32, device=device ) prefill_buffer = torch.empty( (num_tokens, CAPACITY_WIDTH), dtype=torch.int32, device=device ) decode_lens_buffer = torch.empty(1, dtype=torch.int32, device=device) token_to_req_indices = torch.zeros(num_tokens, dtype=torch.int32, device=device) slot_mapping = torch.zeros(num_tokens, dtype=torch.int64, device=device) block_table = torch.zeros((1, 1), dtype=torch.int32, device=device) def run() -> None: build_c128a_topk_metadata( positions, COMPRESS_RATIO, 0, token_to_req_indices, block_table, 2, slot_mapping, global_decode_buffer, decode_lens_buffer, prefill_buffer, max_compressed_tokens=width, ) run() return triton.testing.do_bench(run, warmup=100, rep=500, return_mode="median") print(f"context={CONTEXT_LEN}, capacity={CAPACITY_WIDTH}, active={ACTIVE_WIDTH}") print(f"{'tokens':>8} {'fixed us':>10} {'adaptive us':>12} {'speedup':>8}") for num_tokens in NUM_TOKENS: fixed_ms = benchmark(num_tokens, CAPACITY_WIDTH) adaptive_ms = benchmark(num_tokens, ACTIVE_WIDTH) print( f"{num_tokens:>8} {fixed_ms * 1000:>10.2f} " f"{adaptive_ms * 1000:>12.2f} {fixed_ms / adaptive_ms:>7.2f}x" ) ``` And we can get ```bash context=32768, capacity=8192, active=256 tokens fixed us adaptive us speedup 512 9.22 7.20 1.28x 2048 15.39 7.20 2.14x 8192 44.00 11.30 3.90x 32768 150.56 25.79 5.84x ``` ### Acc GPT 5.6 sol helps doing the acc test as https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52448 mentioned, results below: - Hardware: 2 x NVIDIA B200 allocated by `chg` (physical GPUs 5 and 6). - Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, exact snapshot `7872f01b1d1fe23eabc4c98b48bffcef5a386062`. - Trigger configuration: TP2, expert parallel, DSpark with 7 speculative tokens, greedy draft, prefix caching, breakable CUDA graphs, and `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` graph mode. - Load: concurrency 32, 8 warm-up waves followed by 8 measured waves, 512 requests total. Each request used the issue payload, `temperature=0`, and `max_tokens=16384`. - Issue hit definition: `finish_reason == "length"`, empty content, and no tool calls. - Warm-up: 0/256 hits, 0 errors, 256/256 `tool_calls` finishes. - Measured after the first 256 requests: 0/256 hits, 0 errors, 256/256 `tool_calls` finishes. - Total: 0/512 hits and 0/512 transport/server errors. - Server error scan: zero CUDA, illegal-memory, assertion, graph-error, fatal, or traceback matches. All 512 responses had non-empty content and tool calls using declared tool names with JSON-decodable arguments. Tool-call count was 1 for 75 responses, 4 for 27 responses, and 6 for 410 responses. This validates absence of the specific length-cap/empty-turn failure; it is not a full semantic task-accuracy evaluation. The prompt was 6,543 tokens and the largest prompt-plus-completion was 9,037 tokens. Therefore this run exercised logical C128A width 128 while retaining the capacity row stride 640, rather than falling back to the full-width path. signals.title: [Bugfix][Model] Mistral3: fix image placeholder grid for processor size overrides
signals.text: ## Purpose `Mistral3MultiModalProcessor._get_prompt_updates` currently computes the image placeholder grid via `PixtralHFEncoderInfo.get_patch_grid_size`, which uses `vision_config.image_size` as the max edge. It ignores `mm_processor_kwargs={"size": {"longest_edge": N}}` and any `preprocessor_config.json` whose `size.longest_edge` differs from `vision_config.image_size`, so the placeholder count no longer matches the `pixel_values` geometry emitted by the HF `PixtralProcessor` and inference fails with: ``` RuntimeError: Expected there to be N prompt placeholders corresponding to N image items, but instead found M prompt placeholders! ... ``` This PR derives `ncols`/`nrows` directly from `out_mm_kwargs["image"][item_idx]["pixel_values"].data.shape[-2:]` divided by `patch_size * spatial_merge_size` — the effective post-`Mistral3PatchMerger` grid stride. HF's `PixtralImageProcessor.get_resize_output_image_size` rounds resized dims to a multiple of that stride, so the floor divides are exact. No checkpoint, output-shape, or user-facing API changes. ## Test Plan ``` pre-commit run --files \ vllm/model_executor/models/mistral3.py \ tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_mistral3.py pytest -q tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_mistral3.py ``` ## Test Result - Pre-commit hooks, Ruff, mypy, SPDX, and repository checks: passed. - `tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_mistral3.py`: all cells passed across `mm_processor_kwargs ∈ {{}, {"size":{"longest_edge":1008}}, {"size":{"longest_edge":1288}}}`, image sizes `{(1540,1540), (1536,1187), (2200,1700)}`, `num_imgs ∈ {1, 2}`, and both `kwargs_on_init` modes. - Standalone reproduction on `mistralai/Mistral-Small-3.1-24B-Instruct-2503`: before the patch, requests with a `longest_edge` override raise the "N prompt placeholders … found M" runtime error; after the patch, every case succeeds and the placeholder count matches the raw HF processor's `pixel_values` geometry. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signals.title: [ROCm][Perf] Optimize DeepSeek V4 C4A top-k with AITER
signals.text: ## Summary This replaces the DeepSeek V4 C4A selector's ROCm top-k bottleneck with a correctness-adapted AITER path for short/medium contexts and a graph-safe tuned native fallback for long contexts on gfx950. - Route C4A prefill/decode top-k through the public AITER v0.1.19 operations. - Convert AITER prefill's packed/global indices back to sequence-local indices, preserving the `-1` sentinel. - Treat every vLLM MTP query row independently (`seq_lens.reshape(-1)`, `next_n=1`) so the existing exact 2-D per-token bounds are preserved for `num_speculative_tokens=2,3,4`. - Make the measured gfx950 hybrid selector the default C4A top-k path, with transparent native fallback when AITER is unavailable or slower. - Tune the existing two-launch native split/merge path for gfx950, FP32, `k=1024`, and up to 64 rows. Add a capture-stable specialization for 65-256 rows: three split blocks below 64K active columns and two blocks above it. Shapes above 256 rows select AITER. - Add focused correctness coverage; report the complete 84-shape kernel matrix below. Tracking issue: #41820. ## Relationship to related work This draft is intentionally a more complete superseding alternative to #46172, #50470, and the decode top-k portion of #52878, not an independent repetition of their unconditional decode call-site swaps. This change materially differs in four ways: 1. vLLM supplies exact 2-D `(batch, next_n)` MTP bounds. AITER v0.1.19 consumes 1-D request lengths and reconstructs per-row bounds, so passing the vLLM tensor with the original `next_n` is not equivalent. This patch flattens the exact bounds and calls AITER with `next_n=1`. 2. It covers prefill. AITER returns packed/global prefill indices while vLLM's consumers require sequence-local indices; this patch performs the required localization and preserves padding sentinels. 3. It covers AITER absence, automatic hybrid dispatch, MTP 2/3/4, short rows, packed nonzero row starts, and unordered threshold ties. 4. It includes the 500K/1M fallback design and avoids AITER's persistent multi-block decode path. The native fallback uses separate split and merge launches, so it has no cross-block spin barrier. #46012 also touches the native sampler, but addresses Wave32 LDS build safety; the gfx950 Wave64 performance specialization here is separately gated. The now-closed #52878's batched GEMM and `exp2` changes are orthogonal. Its top-k change routes every decode shape to AITER, whose v0.1.19 decode API is one-block only. Against that unconditional selector, this hybrid has identical kernel latency at 10K and 100K, while improving the long-context geometric mean: | Context | Hybrid / unconditional AITER | Cells faster / total | Range | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 10K | 1.00x | same 21/21 | 1.00-1.00x | | 100K | 1.00x | same 21/21 | 1.00-1.00x | | 500K | 1.21x | 19/21 (1 equal) | 0.98-1.46x | | 1M | 1.76x | 20/21 (1 equal) | 1.00-2.29x | This is why the long, low/mid-row fallback is part of the same standalone change rather than following an unconditional AITER decode switch. ## Kernel A/B Hardware/software: one gfx950 MI355 OAM, Torch `2.12.0+git6bbd260`, HIP `7.2.53211`, amd-aiter `0.1.19`. Production C4A shape is FP32 logits with fixed allocated width `1,048,576 / 4 = 262,144`, `k=1024`, and active compressed length `context / 4`. Each cell uses 20 warmups and 100 HIP-event samples; the reported metric is median speedup over the original vLLM `_C` implementation. `N` below is `num_speculative_tokens`; each request contributes `N + 1` target query rows. All 84 cells passed unordered-set correctness against the reference. ### Eager auto-dispatch speedup #### Context 10K | Batch | N=2 | N=3 | N=4 | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 2.81x | 2.79x | 2.83x | | 2 | 2.82x | 2.76x | 2.78x | | 4 | 2.80x | 2.77x | 2.83x | | 8 | 2.77x | 2.76x | 2.76x | | 16 | 2.74x | 2.78x | 2.75x | | 32 | 2.80x | 2.82x | 2.91x | | 64 | 3.02x | 3.11x | 3.49x | #### Context 100K | Batch | N=2 | N=3 | N=4 | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 2.11x | 2.08x | 2.12x | | 2 | 1.78x | 1.95x | 2.11x | | 4 | 2.11x | 1.61x | 2.13x | | 8 | 1.66x | 1.91x | 1.93x | | 16 | 1.91x | 2.15x | 2.51x | | 32 | 2.59x | 3.06x | 3.63x | | 64 | 3.88x | 4.48x | 4.50x | #### Context 500K | Batch | N=2 | N=3 | N=4 | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 1.12x | 1.12x | 1.11x | | 2 | 1.11x | 1.10x | 1.11x | | 4 | 1.11x | 1.10x | 1.11x | | 8 | 1.10x | 1.24x | 1.24x | | 16 | 1.29x | 1.43x | 1.32x | | 32 | 1.35x | 1.55x | 1.46x | | 64 | 1.58x | 1.76x | 1.69x | #### Context 1M | Batch | N=2 | N=3 | N=4 | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 1.14x | 1.14x | 1.15x | | 2 | 1.14x | 1.13x | 1.14x | | 4 | 1.16x | 1.13x | 1.14x | | 8 | 1.13x | 1.31x | 1.16x | | 16 | 1.17x | 1.29x | 1.18x | | 32 | 1.19x | 1.39x | 1.36x | | 64 | 1.42x | 1.52x | 1.06x | The automatic backend is AITER for all 10K/100K cells. signals.title: [Frontend] Prevent Kimi K3 reserved markers in response text
signals.text: ## Summary - exclude the one-token Kimi K3 reserved marker heads (`<|open|>`, `<|close|>`, and `<|end_of_msg|>`) from response text - apply the same constraint to the Python and Rust frontend structural-tag builders - add grammar behavior coverage for reserved-marker prefixes ## Why Kimi K3 channel markers are multi-token sequences. For example, the tools-open marker is emitted as: ``` <|open|> tools <|sep|> ``` The response body previously excluded only the complete `<|open|>tools<|sep|>` string. `any_text_excluding` masks the token that completes an excluded string, so the matcher could first accept `<|open|>` and `tools` as ordinary response text and reject the transition only when `<|sep|>` was sampled. A real failure followed exactly this path: 1. The model tried to transition into the tools channel by generating `<|open|>tools<|sep|>`. 2. The grammar consumed `<|open|>tools` inside response text. 3. It masked `<|sep|>` after that prefix had already been committed. 4. The model had to choose a different continuation. Observed outputs appended filler such as `工具`, `请稍等`, or a zero-width character, exposing a partial `<|open|>tools...` marker as response content while the tool channel never opened. The same failure mode applies when the model reaches for `<|close|>message<|sep|>`: excluding the complete marker can strand generation after `<|close|>message`. Excluding the one-token reserved heads moves the decision to the first token. `<|open|>` and `<|end_of_msg|>` are blocked inside response text. `<|close|>` remains available through the response tag's valid `<|close|>response<|sep|>` end branch, so accepting it commits the grammar to that boundary before a sibling marker suffix can enter text. ## Related work #51355 covers a broader set of Kimi K3 structured-output fixes and currently uses complete-marker exclusions. This PR isolates the prefix-safe constraint and keeps the Python and Rust frontend builders aligned. ## Testing - `python -m pytest tests/tool_parsers/test_structural_tag_registry.py -k kimi_k3 -q` — 30 passed - `cargo nextest run -p vllm-parser kimi_k3` — 32 passed - Ruff 0.14.0 format and lint checks - `cargo fmt --check` - `git diff --check` ## AI assistance This PR includes code developed with OpenAI Codex assistance. I reviewed the complete diff and validation results.

## Purpose Extend the existing ROCm AITER `fuse_qk_norm_rope_kvcache` compile pass with a gated-QKV pattern. This enables the compile fusion required by gated-attention models including Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and Qwen3.8. signals.title: [Bugfix][V1] Don't crash the engine on an aborted request
signals.text: ## Purpose I think there is a narrow race condition allowing for an uncaught RuntimeError affecting requests aborted before they've started running. A request can be aborted (e.g. when a client disconnect) via `finish_requests` while still sitting in the scheduler's waiting queue. If it lands between `schedule` popping the request and checking its status, the status is no longer WAITING or PREEMPTED, and `schedule` raises an uncaught RuntimeError. This crashes the entire engine-core process. For vllm-omni the single stage dying dying takes the orchestrator and all other stages down with it (which was how I originally found the issue). I'm not 100% certain this is the correct fix but I tried to split the problem into two pieces * An early check right after `peek_request` drops an already finished request but before any KV cache allocation happens for it. * A second at the original crash site handling the narrower window between the (second) pop_request() and the status check For the second in particular I'm not confident the clean up code is entirely correct and would greatly appreciate some feedback. @njhill ## Test Plan - New regression test, test_schedule_drops_request_aborted_while_waiting in tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.pt that simulating the conditions triggering the trash. - Verified the test fails with the original RuntimeError: Invalid request status: FINISHED_ABORTED traceback against unpatched scheduler.py, and passes with the fix. ## Test Result ================= 131 passed, 16 warnings in 67.08s (0:01:07) ==================

signals.title: [Kimi K3][Pref] Export prefill checkpoints in a single FlashKDA pass
signals.text: ## Purpose This PR adds an optional Kimi-K3 prefill checkpoint mode for fine-grained prefix caching. When enabled, FlashKDA exports an intermediate recurrent-state checkpoint during the prefill. The checkpoint is stored in an internal request-owned Mamba block, allowing prefix cache entries smaller than the Mamba block size to be reused without an additional FlashKDA forward. Main changes: - Export recurrent-state checkpoints from the existing packed FlashKDA prefill. - Export the matching causal-conv state. - Support partial prefix caching and spec decoding. - Add internal checkpoint block allocation, lifecycle management, and scheduler metadata. - Allow the scheduler to skip the additional checkpoint-boundary forward. - Add unit tests for checkpoint metadata, block lifecycle, and prefix caching. [#52789](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52789) introduced the prefill-checkpoint infrastructure. This PR adds efficient support for fine-grained partial prefix caching and exports the checkpoint directly from the existing FlashKDA kernel, avoiding an additional or split FlashKDA forward. ## Usage ```bash VLLM_KIMI_K3_KDA_CHECKPOINT_MODE=1 \ vllm serve <model> \ --kda-prefill-backend flashkda \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --mamba-cache-mode align \ --prefix-match-unit 128 ``` This PR depends on [vllm-project/FlashKDA#7](https://github.com/vllm-project/FlashKDA/pull/7). The FlashKDA commit is temporarily pinned and should be updated after that PR is merged. ## Test Plan Setup: - TP8 on 2 × 4 GB300 - Growing prefix from 120K to 164K tokens - +2K tokens per round - 8 concurrent streams - Three runs per variant ## Test Result | Variant | P50 TTFT | **Improvement** | | --- | ---: | ---: | | #52789, non-partial | 2,151.53 ms | Baseline | | #52789, partial128 | 2,375.23 ms | **-10.40%** | | This PR, non-partial | 2,141.67 ms | Baseline | | **This PR, partial128** | **1,398.49 ms** | **34.70%** | ## Correctness Three consecutive full OCRBench runs with checkpoint mode and partial128 produced: 89.4% 89.6% 89.3% mean: 89.43% --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signals.title: [SM100] Hdim 256 optimized
signals.text: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Purpose Re-enables FA4 for `head_size=256` on Blackwell, which was temporarily disabled in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52050 because the SM100 2-CTA hd256 kernel rejected `seqused_q/seqused_k` — something vLLM's decoder attention always supplies. That gap is now closed upstream in https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/180, which adds forward `seqused` support along with hd256 optimizations. This PR reverts #52050 and integrates the kernel properly, with a fallback to FA2 for everything it cannot serve: - The kernel reads paged KV through TMA only, with one page per 128-token tile, so the backend now advertises an exact KV cache block size of 128 for hd256. That 128 is chosen automatically when the user does not pin one; a user-pinned `--block-size` that is not a multiple of 128 makes FLASH_ATTN ineligible for hd256 (an error if the backend was requested explicitly). - `forward()` page-aligns `max_seqlen_k` and slices the block table to match; the over-hang is masked out by `seqused_k`. - The kernel has no SplitKV support, so `num_splits=1` is pinned for this path, and cascade attention is disabled. - Selection falls back to FA2 for attention sinks, logits soft capping, mm_prefix, R-SWA and DCP. In practice Gemma-2 (soft capping) and multimodal Gemma-3 (mm_prefix) keep using FA2, while Gemma-1, text-only Gemma-3 and PaliGemma/ColPali get FA4. - The hd256 kernel is opt-in (`supports_fa4_hd256`), so callers that do not build the required call shape — ViT/`mm_encoder_attention`, turboquant, MLA prefill — keep resolving to FA2. - Only `(head_size=256, head_size_v=256)` uses this kernel; `(head_size=256, head_size_v=128)` still takes generic FA4, exactly as it did before #52050. Sliding window on the decoder path is enabled again, since the kernel handles it; encoder inputs (dense `cu_seqlens_k`, no `seqused_k`) still fall back to FA2. ## Test Plan ```bash pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_attention_selector.py pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_flash_attn.py -k fa4_hd256 pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_flash_attn.py # reproducer from #52050 pytest tests/models/multimodal/pooling/test_colpali.py::test_colpali_multimodal_text_query_image_docs ``` ## Test Result On B200 (SM100): ``` tests/kernels/attention/test_attention_selector.py 52 passed, 10 skipped tests/kernels/attention/test_flash_attn.py -k fa4_hd256 8 passed ``` --- AI assistance was used for the vLLM-side changes. I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests reported above.

signals.title: [Bugfix][MoE] Tune FlashInfer experts to scheduler token limit
signals.text: ## Summary - pass vLLM's parallel-aware maximum token bucket to FlashInfer CUTLASS experts - fix the same omitted or hardcoded bound in modular BF16, BF16 LoRA, and MXINT4 expert paths - cover the CUTLASS forwarding behavior with a focused regression assertion ## Root cause These expert paths let FlashInfer use its default `tune_max_num_tokens=8192`, even when vLLM's effective MoE input bound was larger. As a result, startup autotuning stopped at 8,192 tokens and larger prefill batches reused a tactic selected for the smaller bucket. The other FlashInfer TRT-LLM expert implementations already use `fi_moe_largest_bucket(self.moe_config)`, which accounts for both `max_num_tokens` and the data-parallel factor while preserving 8,192 as the minimum tuning range. This change applies the same bound consistently to the remaining paths. ## Duplicate-work check I checked issue #41306 and searched open PRs for `41306 in:body`, `FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE autotune`, and `tune_max_num_tokens FlashInfer`. No open PR addresses this omission. This follows up on #46838, which removed the unrelated CUDA graph capture size as the tuning bound, and #47427, which introduced the shared parallel-aware helper but did not update every expert path. ## Evaluation The motivating B300 dummy-load run used `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384`, but both FP8 and BF16 FlashInfer routed-MoE autotune caches contained 21 buckets ending at 8,192. This draft fixes that coverage mismatch; an end-to-end post-change performance rerun is still pending. Validation completed: - commit-time pre-commit suite: passed, including Ruff, formatting, mypy, SPDX, import, and configuration checks - `python -m pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_flashinfer_moe.py -k params_are_forwarded -q`: 2 passed with FlashInfer 0.6.17 - `python -m pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_trtllm_bf16_moe.py -q`: 3 passed with FlashInfer 0.6.18.dev20260807 - focused MXINT4 wrapper test: 1 passed with FlashInfer 0.6.18.dev20260807 - mocked BF16 LoRA invocation: confirmed `tune_max_num_tokens=16384` is forwarded The pinned-0.6.17 BF16 suite rerun was interrupted during its cold native JIT build and should be completed before marking this ready for review. ## AI assistance Codex was used to investigate, implement, validate, and draft this change. The human submitter must review every changed line and complete the remaining validation before marking the PR ready. Related: #41306

signals.title: [K3] Optimize K3 recover ssm kernel times
signals.text: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Purpose PR #51855 added an option to use the ReplaySSM-like recover method. But the new approach, although improving memory footprint and so occupancy, actually hurt run time. The approach should be faster, but it is simple triton vs highly optimized non-triton. Here we make some small tweaks to improve the new output-only verify kernel and the kda and convolution end-of-step commit kernels. ## Test Plan No new tests. This just changes kernel internals and reorders two kernels so are covered by existing tests. We also wrote some one-off checkers that, on fake input, found the output within expected numerical differences (due to changes in associativity) from the old kernels. @benchislett has run e2e tests. ## Test Result @benchislett to add correctness results. On perf, small speed improvements, about half a millisecond per step on batches 1,8,32,and 3ms on batch 128. --- We make a few simple changes that result in a substantial speedup. ### For commit: The biggest is that we change the KDA recover from a backward recurrence to a forward recurrence, which is the bulk of the speedup. This also lets us save register state when operating in ALIGN_MODE (for prefix caching). We reorder the computation to go plan -> kda commit -> conv commit, vs the more natural plan -> conv commit -> kda commit, and then add PDL between kda and conv. This lets us overlap kda with conv, especially as while they both depend on plan, neither depends on the other for inputs and they have separate outputs. And as kda blocks are longer-tailed the re-reordering is beneficial. However, because commit does not run with cuda graphs, the PDL could hurt more in host overhead than it helps, so we do not enable it. Lastly, for both kernels we retune num-warps and the number of output elements each handles. ALIGNED_MODE on and off want slightly different values. PDL does not impact the preferred values. To guide optimization we wrote a microbenchmark (not submitted) and optimized for B300, matching the original PRs experiment. We can only match the original PR numbers if we assume that the original PR was actually run with the kernels in unaligned mode. Our microbenchmark assumes TP=8, times the span from plan start to end of the second of conv or kda commit, simulates cold and hot L2 cache inputs, and runs with a cuda graph and CUPTI timing. Although commit does not run under a cuda graph, using one is the best way to get consistent, low-noise timings. For ease of experimentation we had all requests uniform in terms of # accepted (using 5 below, slightly higher than the 4.2 average in the e2e nsys measurements in the original PR), and also uniform in bondary behavior. We observed runtime affine in # accepted, as expected (not shown). We ran in either unaligned, aligned with no boundary crossed, or aligned with boundary crossed at the second token. The latter case would never happen at larger batches, we would expect a mix of aligned and unaligned, but it shows the costs. We get about 2x speedup across batches and align modes, more at the more production relevant aligned but no boundary. Note due to how vLLM groups KDA layers that share block tables, the commit kernels (plan, commit kda, compact conv, etc.) are launched on 5 or 4 layers at a time, not all 69 as you'd hope. I have a follow-on commit that groups them together which helps time further, especially as nsys shows the lack of cuda graphs causes substantial gaps at smaller batches. Results below, times are plan -> kda commit -> conv compact span. Small batch, with only 5 layers per invocation, is largely launch bound and so not much improvement is possible, and even larger batches there is not that much work. You can see more than 2x speedup at larger batches. Experimenting with the kernels at 69 layers at a time, we found grouping would improve total time for all layers by 3x for batch 1, 1.2x at batch 32, and 1.05x at batch 256 (not shown). Mode | B1 | B32 | B256 | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Unaligned | 13.22 → 12.22 (1.08x) | 110.63 → 64.48 (1.72x) | 827.68 → 440.01 (1.88x) | | Aligned, no boundary | 14.11 → 13.07 (1.08x) | 160.10 → 76.49 (2.09x) | 1319.62 → 551.87 (2.39x) | | Aligned, boundary at accepted token 2 | 14.31 → 13.74 (1.04x) | 168.66 → 87.14 (1.94x) | 1421.05 → 646.39 (2.20x) | ### For verify: Small changes here but surprisingly worth a lot. We had a similar microbenchmark as above but for verify. PDL surprisingly hurts us, so we report only the kernel time, not the span, although we ran and timed the conv1d -> verify span. We hoisted dt_bias out of the loop, which resulted in enough code gen change to be worth a win. Then we retuned the value-slice and num_warp params. We found value-slice should vary with batch size, which is typical as smaller value slices are less efficient but better saturate the machine if there isn't enough work. And that num-warps should be 1 everywhere. Also added some cache hints as state and V are not shared across blocks (value slicing) but everything else is. Here are timings, again B300, TP=8, with T=8 and gate_lower_bound=5.0: | Batch | Old | New | Speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 13.79 µs | 8.98 µs | 1.54× | | 2 | 13.95 µs | 9.38 µs | 1.49× | | 4 | 14.24 µs | 10.08 µs | 1.41× | | 8 | 15.46 µs | 13.22 µs | 1.17× | | 16 | 27.46 µs | 18.98 µs | 1.45× | | 32 | 41.55 µs | 34.40 µs | 1.21× | | 64 | 79.49 µs | 63.49 µs | 1.25× | | 128 | 147.89 µs | 111.50 µs | 1.33× | | 256 | 306.19 µs | 233.17 µs | 1.31× | | 512 | 632.17 µs | 494.05 µs | 1.28× | Surprises: Passing gate lower bound does change the results a little. As noted above, PDL does not help. A tiny bit in some places but regresses enough others that I left it off, vs making it a heuristic. I also spent a while trying to get a good result with a full chunk/prefill-style UT transform, in Triton, having had good results with that for Mamba-2 layers. Whether due to the per-channel decay (unlikely) or the triangular inverse (likely), I found many bad ways to write it, and with a lot of work I got a version that (for T=8) only tied the recurrence above. I expected big wins, but Triton limitations make it quite challenging. I'm sure in CuTe it'd be very fast. As is, it would have the cost and benefit that the runtime would be independent of T. But as it is much more complicated, and as T=8 is probably more of an upper than lower bound for draft_length + 1, better to stick with the recurrence. AI Declaration: AI assisted in the writing of this code, but I have reviewed every line. Full disclosure, I reviewed all the code in the PR, but the one-off microbenchmarks and such I did not look at too carefully. <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [x] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [x] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [x] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details> **BEFORE SUBMITTING, PLEASE READ <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing>** (anything written below this line will be removed by GitHub Actions)

signals.title: Fix MNNVL Lamport mailbox publication and cleanup
signals.text: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Purpose Fix silent output corruption in vLLM's MNNVL Lamport all-gather and reduce-scatter. CUDA multicast addresses may only be written with `multimem.*`, so mailbox payloads use a relaxed, system-scope multicast store ([PTX ISA](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#data-movement-and-conversion-instructions-multimem-ld-reduce-multimem-st-multimem-red)). The payload words are also the readiness signal: volatile readers reject stale or partially visible values containing the Lamport sentinel and retry, so release/acquire ordering and `fence.proxy.alias` are unnecessary. Also fix triple-buffer cleanup. The current `(epoch + 1) % 3` rule can erase epoch N+1 after a faster peer publishes it while another rank is still finishing epoch N; cleaning `(epoch + 2) % 3` targets the previously consumed stage instead. DeepSeek-V4 with MegaMoE, expert parallelism, and TP8 across two four-GPU GB300 hosts reaches these kernels through sequence-parallel all-gather and reduce-scatter. Current K3 and DeepSeek-V4 with expert parallelism disabled do not enter this path. Open-PR searches for MNNVL Lamport, multicast publication, and mailbox-stage cleanup found no duplicate fix. ## Test Plan Run the new test in the two-GPU B200 Distributed job, which provides the required CUDA multicast mapping: ```bash pytest -v -s \ tests/distributed/test_custom_all_gather_reduce_scatter.py ``` The test asserts a real CUDA multicast mapping and constructs a reachable one-epoch skew using the existing per-rank epoch metadata and mailbox stages. It invokes the shipping all-gather and reduce-scatter kernels, verifies the fast rank's N+1 publication arrived, then asserts that the slow rank's epoch-N cleanup preserves it. ## Test Result - Two-GPU GB300 production-kernel test: old `+1` cleanup erased both all-gather and reduce-scatter N+1 publications in 20/20 cycles; fixed `+2` retained both in 20/20. The final pytest covers all three stage rotations, fails on old code, and passes on fixed code. - Two-node GB300 TP8 DeepSeek-V4 with expert parallelism, MegaMoE, CUDA graphs, CUMEM/MNNVL, and custom collectives: sky-color 10/10 and bat-and-ball 10/10 before load, 128/128 correct concurrent requests, then both probes 10/10 again. - CUDA 13.2 codegen is identical on SM100 and SM103: plain CUDA C++ emits weak `STG.E.128`, while `multimem.st.relaxed.sys` emits `STG.E.128.STRONG.SYS`. Release plus proxy-fence added three memory barriers and was therefore removed. - A final two-host, eight-rank stress completed 2,000 epochs with zero mismatches for both weak and multicast stores on current GB300 hardware. The multicast spelling is retained because ordinary access to a multicast mapping remains undefined by PTX; the deterministic red/green regression is the independently reproducible stage-lifecycle bug. AI assistance was used during investigation and implementation; the human submitter reviewed the change and owns the design and validation. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose and root cause are described. - [x] The test plan provides the exact real-GPU test command. - [x] The test results include deterministic regression and end-to-end validation. - [x] Documentation impact was considered; the code and test describe this kernel-only change. </details> **BEFORE SUBMITTING, PLEASE READ <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing>** (anything written below this line will be removed by GitHub Actions)
